text:
The Restore Britain Budget.

Britain has spent decades being governed by politicians who believe the answer to every problem is yet more government - that policy has destroyed our country.

More spending. More borrowing. More regulation. More taxes. More state.

Parasitic overreach into our lives - delivered by politicians and civil servants who have no understanding or appreciation of how real wealth and opportunity is generated in the private sector.

And what have the British people received in return?

A country where working families struggle. Where businesses face punishing costs. Where young people cannot afford homes. Where failing public services demand ever more money, whilst prioritising endless third world migrants. Where inflation runs rampant.

For British men and women, it is a government-backed scam. Corrupt incompetence.

It is impossible for Britain to tax itself into prosperity. I repeat, IMPOSSIBLE.

Wealth is created by people - the public sector should exist to support the private sector, not the reverse and that is the principle which underpins our philosophy.

Restore Britain backs the farmer producing food, the white van man driving the economy, the engineer designing machinery, the shopkeeper serving customers and the entrepreneur risking everything to start a business.

It comes down to this - Restore Britain will protect their freedom to succeed.

If you work hard and contribute, we are on your side.

Our Budget would begin the work of returning power, responsibility and money to the British people.

First, the spending cuts - to come before ANY reductions in tax.

Our 20 point plan to restore prosperity…

1. Freeze working-age benefit rates.

We will freeze working-age benefit rates for the duration of the first Parliament. Britain cannot indefinitely increase expenditure without considering the burden on the people funding it. That would be morally wrong. The healthy indolent will not be rewarded.

2. Restrict welfare eligibility.

No more benefits for foreigners, saving billions. No need to expand.

3. Reform sickness and disability benefits

We will overhaul eligibility, assessment procedures and return-to-work support.

People with serious disabilities and health conditions must receive appropriate protection.

But those who can work, will work. If they refuse, they will be put to work. That simple.

4. Reform pensions.

We will protect the State Pension while replacing the triple lock with annual CPI uprating. Public-sector pension arrangements will be overhauled to address differences with private-sector provision.

These measures will save tens of billions - all outlined in full in our economic paper, The Wealth Of Our Nation.

Next, take an axe to unnecessary government spending

5. The quango bonfire.

We will conduct a comprehensive review of arm's-length public bodies, the default will be abolish unless there is a serious reason to retain. Where its functions duplicate a government department, consolidate them. Deliver accountability and savings. AI will mean vast cuts are possible.

A LOT of Whitehall civil servants will lose their jobs. To be frank.

6. Freeze most departmental budgets.

We will introduce a three-year nominal spending freeze across most government departments - the main exception will be our programme of mass deportations, which in the short term will cost, however as we know, any immediate funds will be quickly recovered and then some.

7. End public spending on Net Zero.

We will end all public expenditure directed towards achieving Net Zero. Energy security will be our main priority. We will support investment in dependable domestic energy supplies, including the infrastructure needed to maintain a resilient electricity system. Energy security will be placed above any ideological dogma. If it makes Britain more resilient, we will pursue it.

8. Review government consultancy and discretionary expenditure.

We will audit consultancy contracts, procurement services, and ALL external advisory work - spending that cannot demonstrate a clear public benefit should end.

The procurement scam will end.

All bullshit ESG and social value nonsense will be stripped away - if the public sector wants to use a third party firm, make it the best one - subject to right-to-work checks to ensure no illegals are being employed.

As stated - spending cuts first, then tax cuts. Done carefully and responsibly. Here’s an overview of how a Restore Britain Government will lift the tax burden…

9. Raise the income tax personal allowance to £16,000.

Nobody should be paying income tax on their first £16,000 of earnings.

We will raise the personal allowance and extend the basic-rate income tax band to £100,000.

We will also restore the full personal allowance to higher earners, ending the withdrawal that creates exceptionally high effective marginal tax rates.

Success will be rewarded, hard work will be rewarded, ambition will be rewarded.

10. Cut corporation tax.

We will introduce a zero corporation tax rate on the first £50,000 of company profits.

Above that threshold, we will restore the headline rate to 19%, with a longer-term ambition of 15%. As soon as fiscal conditions allow.

Let’s give small businesses the genuine breathing room to get their operation off the ground, and then use the corporation tax cut to compete with our neighbours.

11. Abolish inheritance tax and stamp duty.

Families should not be punished for saving, investing and passing assets to their children.

We will abolish inheritance tax.

For farmers, for family businesses, for everyone.

The state has no claim to a family's lifetime of accumulated wealth simply because somebody has died. I detest it. It will be binned for all.

Stamp duty makes moving home more expensive, discourages mobility and creates unnecessary friction in the housing market.

We will abolish it.

12. Reduce disruptive tax.

We will cut the standard rate of VAT from 20% to 18%.

We will also raise the VAT registration threshold to £150,000, helping smaller businesses grow without immediately facing additional tax burden. The amount of businesses hovering just under the current threshold is painful. The issue is OBVIOUS, yet nobody in government has thought to act.

And we will ditch unnecessary taxes.

We will abolish:
Insurance Premium Tax.
Air Passenger Duty.
The Climate Change Levy.
The UK Emissions Trading Scheme.

We will also substantially increase the annual Capital Gains Tax exemption.

Restore Britain’s objective is a tax system that is simpler, more predictable and less hostile to investment.

Next, we will restore a state that works for our people.

13. Hold the NHS accountable.

The NHS will remain free at the point of use for British citizens.

We propose charging non-citizens at market rates - ensuring they actually pay the bills.

We will make private healthcare expenditure tax deductible. If people want to go private, let’s make it cheaper.

Alongside far-reaching structural reform, we will demand basic improvements in patient communication. Answer the telephone. Confirm referrals. Explain test results. Keep patients informed. Use AI to clear pressure on GPs.

All patient-facing staff must demonstrate the English-language communication skills necessary to perform their roles safely. If staff can’t speak English to the required standard, they will no longer have a job.

14. Restore Britain’s education system.

We will move towards greater school-level autonomy, with funding more closely linked to pupil numbers.

We will remove VAT from private education and make private education tax deductible.

We will also promote practical education, apprenticeships and stronger links between schools and employers. The aim will be to prepare children for working adulthood - full paper to come.

Apprenticeships are vital - my businesses have developed hundreds and hundreds. It works, especially with the rise of AI.

Student loan interest abolished for British nationals resident in the UK, full paper published.

An overhaul of childcare regulation and funding - led by those in the sector who know what’s necessary and what’s not.

Next.

The Restore Britain Budget will work to restore a self-sufficient Britain, backed by sovereign AI capabilities.

15. Support British farming and food security.

We will review the regulatory and tax burdens facing British farmers.

Food security must be recognised as a matter of national resilience and urgency. That will be central to everything.

We will make it FAR easier for domestic producers to compete for public-sector food contracts and examine ways to reduce unnecessary administration. Let’s use the public sector spend to back our own people, not import from foreign farmers.

Britain should not become increasingly dependent on imported food while making it harder for its own farmers to survive. And we desperately need to bring more young people into the industry…

16. Ease pressure on transport network.

We will rebuild Britain's transport network, tackling potholes, congestion and crumbling infrastructure while improving vital freight routes and rural roads - motorists will no longer be treated as cash cows. Fuel duty cut, and plenty more. (Full paper about to be published.)

Get this right, and the whole economy is lubricated.

17. Back small businesses.

We will review regulations introduced over recent decades, with a presumption in favour of removing law. Compliance simplified, licensing stripped back. Administrative burdens burned away. Scrap IR35, obviously.

Business rates abolished for small high street businesses. Review car park charges. Boost police numbers in town centres.

Restore confidence on the high street. Bring footfall back. Watch businesses thrive.

18. Develop sovereign AI capability.

AI is coming whether we like it or not. We need to ensure that we have our own protected AI capability which can promote and defend our own interests. We’re already falling behind, and it’s getting worse. We have the opportunity to be a genuine world-leader. Let’s pursue it.

19. A foreign policy that puts Britain’s interests first.

No endless foreign wars driving up the cost of living for ordinary families, no foreign aid unless explicitly to advance our interests. We will prioritise national security, trade, energy independence and protecting British citizens abroad.

Spending will be increased, but our armed forces exist to defend Britain and our vital national interests, not to act as the world's policeman.

20. Protect sound money and fiscal stability. This is the most important of all.

We will pursue a balanced Budget over the medium term and a declining debt-to-GDP ratio. Our aim is to cut the debt, not just the deficit.

The era of mass money printing will end. Inflation will be controlled. The cost-of-living reduced.

The aim - a Britain that belongs to its people

Every Budget promises change, while the state grows larger and the taxpayer becomes poorer.

Restore Britain offers a completely different direction.

A smaller government that spends less - all helped by a massive reduction in the number of migrants living in Britain.

Doing a small list of things, but doing them well.

A welfare state that protects genuine need and expects personal responsibility.

A tax system that rewards work, saving and enterprise.

Public services that answer to the people who fund them.

An economy built on productive businesses rather than a parasitic state.

We do not believe the British people need politicians to manage every aspect of their lives.

We believe they need the freedom to build better lives for themselves.

In short - we will stop buying votes with other people’s money.

Our ambition is not to make government richer.

It is to restore the prosperity of the British economy, the British nation and the British people.

It's about time that you (and many others like you) start to accept the Chareidim for who they are -- and look at the contributions that they make both to the Jewish world AND the State of Israel that no one else makes.

And then, at that point, you can ask a more important question.  

What contributions do the Chareidim make that I (and others like me) can benefit from.  Let me open myself up to them.

[I will NOT list them here -- if you want to see them, then you will have to take the time to look for them].

And what contributions do I (and others like me) make that the Chareidim can benefit from.  Let me offer it to them and they will decide whether or not they want to open themselves up to them.

That is actual Achdus.

And that is in line with the vision of the Jewish people that has existed for as far back as the 5 books of Moses -- and can be found in the Neviim and beyond.

---

And there is one other point that finally needs to be stated loud and clear -- since you (and others like you) constantly focus on the Chareidim.

Zionism has had many successes -- but stopping anti-semitism and protecting Jews from the murderous onslaught of the antisemite is not one of them.

And yet - that was the prediction.

Herzl told us that the solution to antisemitism was having a state like any other state.

We were told that an army would put fear into the antisemite.

That if we won the wars the arabs would finally make peace (this was partly true, but not true enough to matter).

And more.  

The State of Israel and the IDF have over and over again been remarkable.  Brave, innovative, creative, daring --- and much more.  

The list or impressive successes is too large to list.

But, at the end of the day, the antisemite is able to murder Jews in numbers surpassed in modern times only by the Holocaust and the pogroms of the Russian revolution.

That is hardly a success.  

In short, at the end of the day -- results matter.
And in the REAL WORLD -- when the results aren't there you ask why.

What do we need to change.
What isn't working.

Is it that we don't have enough military might?

Is it that we haven't been willing to compromise on a political solution.

Is it that we haven't been willing to make our case in the media? [you, and others like you, have been AMAZING in this role].

Is it that our economy is not strong enough?

I could go on.

In short, the solution does not seem to be more political power.  
Or economic power.  
Or media influence.  

And yet -- you (and others like you) constantly circle this wagon.

It's time for a change.
A real change.

It's time to recognize that we have ALWAYS been 12 tribes.

With 12 different world views.
And 12 different contributions.

And ONE of those tribes was dedicated to the service in the Beis HaMikdash (at the heart of which was the Torah and the Luchos HaBris).

That they were exempt from military service.
And they were not given the same economic means as the rest of the nation.

And that there was a RELATIONSHIP between them and the rest of the nation -- and between the rest of the nation and them [see, for example -- that wondrous warrior Dovid HaMelech and his love and respect for the Leviim, Kohanim and the Beis HaMikdash, which he so desired to build].

In short -- it's time that we all stop trying to force each other to be us.  
To mold each other in our image.  

That's the road to division and more failure.

It's time to recognize that the zionist project -- for all its wonders -- did not get everything right.  

And that we are in as much (if not greater) danger today than we have been in a long time.

And that it does NOT provide the JEWISH path forward for the Jewish people.

And it's time for the Chareidim to recognize the wonders that the zionist movement has produced.  

The hospitals it has built (although the Chareidim have also built their own hospitals).

The land they have built up (although the Chareidim actually started that BEFORE there was a zionist project).

The economy they have built.

And more.

It's time for real achdus.
And it's time to come to grips with the BIBLICAL vision of a Jewish society.  Some of which we have.  And some of which we need to still work on implementing.

I wish us ALL much success.

@RahulGandhi, as a stakeholder affected by the NH-709A upgradation, I believe this case raises serious questions about accountability in public infrastructure.

In Tata Projects Ltd. v. Union of India & Ors., Writ-C No. 4559/2025, the Allahabad High Court’s judgment dated 08.07.2026 recorded significant findings:

• Land handover: NHAI’s contractual obligations included providing at least 90% of the required Right of Way in contiguous stretches of at least 5 km. The Court examined the serious dispute over whether effective, hindrance-free possession had been provided.

• Non-compliance with court directions: Despite specific directions to provide date-wise details of land possession, NHAI failed to do so; the Court described its conduct as “contumacious.”

• Engineer’s report overlooked: The Authority’s Engineer had sought a 248-day extension citing impediments. The Court found that the decision-making process failed to properly consider material on record.

• No application of mind: The show-cause notice and termination order were virtually verbatim, while Tata Projects’ detailed reply was not adequately considered.

• Arbitrary State action: The Court emphasised that NHAI, as a State authority under Article 12, must act fairly and reasonably. It found the impugned action arbitrary and an unfair practice.

The High Court consequently quashed the termination order, forfeiture of bank guarantees and fresh tender dated 03.02.2025. It directed a joint site inspection and efforts to agree on a completion timeline, taking account of the Engineer’s reports and contractual framework. Tata Projects had offered to complete the remaining work within 14 months.

The subsequent Supreme Court proceedings must be respected: the High Court’s relief is subject to the Supreme Court’s orders, and the matter remains sub judice. But the underlying questions of land handover, reasoned decision-making and accountability cannot simply be wished away.

Meanwhile, the NH-709A project remains a matter of concern for affected businesses, travellers and the public purse, with delay and escalating costs carrying consequences beyond the contracting parties.

Why should businesses and the public bear the cost of administrative failures and prolonged contractual disputes? Who is accountable for a time-bound resolution and completion of this critical highway?

This is not about favouring one corporate house over another. It is about the rule of law, fair treatment of businesses, responsible use of taxpayers’ money and infrastructure delivered in the public interest.

text:
Palestinians Feel Humiliated

Palestinians frequently complain that the establishment of the Jewish state and the continuing Jewish governing of the Palestinian people and of Palestine act as a humiliation to them. Their feelings of being humiliated do not mean that Israel has humiliated them in any deliberate way. 

A sports team that severely underplays against a stronger opponent offers a clear analogy, because the winning side simply went out and competed while the weaker side brought the result on itself through repeated errors and poor decisions on the field. The opponent never set out to embarrass anyone and never planned its victory as a form of personal degradation. Israel did not set out to humiliate Palestinians, and it does not govern its historic homeland, including the heartland of Judea and Samaria, for the purpose of humiliating them. 

Israel established a state and continues to govern its land because the land belongs to the Jewish people and because Jews have the right to live there under their own sovereignty after centuries of exile. Palestinians themselves choose how they relate to those facts every day.

It remains quite understandable that Palestinians feel humiliated once their consistent mistakes over many decades have produced utter defeat and a steady reduction in their practical options. When any people make poor choices that keep leading to continuous degradation of their freedom and to the blocking of their stated aspirations, embarrassment and a sense of humiliation follow naturally from the outcomes they have created through their own actions.

text:
The Battle of White Plains occurred on October 28, 1776, as part of the larger New York campaign during the American Revolutionary War. Following earlier American defeats at Long Island and the British occupation of New York City, General George Washington withdrew his Continental Army northward through Westchester County. His goal was to protect supply lines, avoid encirclement, and maintain a viable fighting force against the superior British army under General William Howe. By late October, Washington had established a defensive position near the village of White Plains, fortifying a series of ridges and hills to block further British advances.

Washington arrayed roughly thirteen thousand troops along a line facing south, with his right flank resting on the elevated ground of Chatterton Hill across the Bronx River. This position offered natural advantages but left the hill somewhat exposed and held by a mix of Continental regulars and militia. Howe, commanding a force of similar or greater size that included British regulars and Hessian auxiliaries, advanced from the south in deliberate columns. Rather than striking the strongly fortified American center, the British commander identified Chatterton Hill as the vulnerable point in the American line and directed his main effort there after preliminary skirmishing.

On the morning of the battle, American outposts delayed the British approach before falling back. Hessian troops under Colonel Johann Rall, supported by British infantry and artillery, crossed the Bronx River under fire and assaulted the hill. Initial American resistance, including artillery fire and musket volleys from troops commanded by officers such as Alexander McDougall and John Haslet, checked the first advances. However, repeated assaults eventually dislodged the militia on the far right of the American position. As the line on Chatterton Hill began to unravel, Washington ordered a general withdrawal to prevent the destruction of his army, with Delaware troops covering the retreat.

Although the British secured Chatterton Hill and claimed a tactical victory, Washington’s main force escaped with relatively moderate losses and remained intact. American casualties numbered roughly two hundred killed, wounded, or missing, while British and Hessian losses were somewhat higher. The engagement forced the Continental Army to continue its retreat into New Jersey, yet it also demonstrated that Washington could conduct an orderly withdrawal under pressure. By preserving the core of his army rather than risking annihilation, the battle helped sustain the revolutionary cause through a difficult campaign season, setting the stage for later American recoveries.

Published January 5, 2003 - 6:20 p.m.
A year has passed since President Kim Dae-jung and North Korean leader Kim Jong-il held the first-ever summit meeting between North and South Korea.

South Korean corporations wholeheartedly welcomed the historic talks, thinking it could give them the inside track to the North's human and natural resources, as well as its market.

At the end of last year, the two Koreas reached a series of agreements on double tax prevention, investment guarantees, dispute resolution mechanisms and payment clearance. The agreements are awaiting ratification by the National Assembly.

But economic cooperation between the two Koreas has brought no more than a trickle of investment in the North. Not a single direct investment has been made between the two countries since the summit. In fact, most South Korean companies are cautious about getting too deeply involved with Pyongyang.

"We are not expanding our business projects in North Korea because inter-Korean relations are unstable and North Korea's intentions are unclear," said an official of LG Electronics Inc., which is leading the LG Group's North Korean project.

According to the Ministry of Unification, 152 South Korean companies are operating original equipment manufacturers in the North. Some small and medium-sized South Korean companies are expanding their role there, and corporations that received direct investment permits before the summit have completed their manufacturing plants there.

The Unification Church completed an auto repair factory near Pyongyang last September, and Taechang has opened a mineral water factory near Mount Kumgang.

And some other companies, while still not willing to invest directly in the North, are continuing to expand their interests there.

Trade extended well past the border of Rome’s empire, which was millions of square miles. Trade routes also existed to India and China. Archaeology has found many pottery sherds from the far east. The merchants were made rich by buying, selling, and trading goods with Rome.

Call To God’s People (18:4-8)
Another voice calls out from heaven for God’s people to come out from her. This is a prophetic reference from Jeremiah and Isaiah’s ministries.

Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea, declare this with a shout of joy, proclaim it, send it out to the end of the earth; say, “The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!” (Isaiah 48:20 ESV)Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her; purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the LORD. (Isaiah 52:11 ESV)“Flee from the midst of Babylon; let every one save his life! Be not cut off in her punishment, for this is the time of the LORD’s vengeance, the repayment he is rendering her. Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunken; the nations drank of her wine; therefore the nations went mad. (Jeremiah 51:6–7 ESV)

The call of the voice from heaven is for the people of God to remove themselves from the ways and immoralities of Rome. Do not participate in the sinfulness of that world. Otherwise, you will share in the plagues that are coming upon Rome and her empire. The judgment of the seven bowls showed seven plagues being poured out on the beast and its throne. God gives an important warning. If you act like the world, you will be judged with the world. Come out from the world and separate yourselves from the Roman ways and sins. They have heaped up their sins as high as the heavens and God has remembered those sins. God is going to pay her back. God is going to pay her double for her deeds. This is just because its sins were so severe that it not only affect them, but also carried the whole world into sinfulness with its idolatry and paganism. God calls for a double portion to be mixed for her in the cup. Recall that we saw this cup as the cup of God’s anger poured full strength (Revelation 14:10). The voice from heaven says that we need to make it a double. Double up the portion in the cup of God’s anger.

Verses 7-8 continue to explain why God’s wrath is so violent against Rome and her empire. Rome glorified itself and lived in luxury. No one gave glory to God for their prosperity. They elevated themselves and glorified themselves. Further, they think they will never fall. They think that these times will never change. They think this prosperity will never end because they think they did it all. They rule and think that rule will never end. God says in verse 8 that this is the reason that they will be struck down suddenly. Rather than life and prosperity, the empire will crumble into death, mourning, and famine. Revelation is not predicting that Rome fell in one day, just as the scriptures are not predicting other nations falling in one day (cf. Isaiah 47:9). It is a symbol of the suddenness of the loss of power and authority. It would seem that the empire would never end and suddenly the empire will be in trouble. It will lose its power and be destroyed. This is the imagery of the fire. Revelation is not predicting Rome literally burning (cf. Isaiah 47:14). The fire is a symbol of judgment. Its time of glory and rule is over. The empire has fallen. Rome has lost her power.

Before we leave verses 4-8 we must see this paragraph contains very important messages for our country. The parallels are very strong. We are full of prosperity and wealth just like Rome. Most live in wasteful, luxurious living just like Rome. Our country shows the same arrogance in thinking that it is the world power that will never fall. Certainly the sins of our nation are heaped as high as heaven. The more this nation turns people away from the true God to worship false gods and religions, the closer we come to meeting the same judgment that Rome met for its sins.

text:
Brakes my heart to have to post this. I was fluent in French & immersed in the French culture before I knew English...  but if you carefully think of it, most in the analysis below is accurate & correct, am afraid. 

THE STATUTE OF LIBERTY MAY BE FRANCE'S ONLY GOOD IDEA - The Wall Street Journal 

The country that gave us the guillotine, terrorism, Marxism, wealth taxes and riots in the streets.

The Statue of Liberty, France’s gift to the American people, was dedicated in New York Harbor on Oct. 28, 1886. Her formal name, “Liberty Enlightening the World,” honored the American Revolution, which France backed with money, ships and soldiers.

Unfortunately, some of France’s other gifts have been far less helpful. For more than 200 years, French intellectuals have presumed to speak for humanity. Too often humanity listened, to its detriment. French ideas have led to the toppling of monarchies and the arming of revolutionaries, and they fill the reading lists of Western universities. Many of these ideas were offered as doctrines of liberation but ended in tragedy. Now the bill has arrived in France, and Americans should read it closely.

The pattern was set in the late 18th century, when the philosophes argued that reason could remake society and the revolutionaries took them at their word. In August 1789, France’s National Constituent Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Four years later the revolution had executed the king and passed the Law of Suspects, under which French citizens could be jailed for their presumed sympathies. Some 17,000 people were executed during the Reign of Terror. The American Revolution produced the Constitution. The French one produced the guillotine.

In “Reflections on the Revolution in France” (1790), Edmund Burke predicted that a general would seize control of the French republic. Napoleon Bonaparte obliged.

A lasting export was a set of assumptions: that an enlightened vanguard may act in the people’s name, that the state can remake society from above, and that legitimacy is settled in the street. The Bolsheviks modeled themselves on the Jacobins. The word “terrorism” entered the English lexicon from the Reign of Terror.

Fast-forward to the 19th century. In 1844 at the Café de la Régence in Paris, a young Karl Marx began his collaboration with Friedrich Engels, which led to “The Communist Manifesto.” Engels recounted that Marx later despaired at what his French disciples made of his work, declaring that he himself was no Marxist.

In the 20th century, Paris became a finishing school for revolutionaries. A young Ho Chi Minh spoke at the 1920 Tours Congress, which founded the French Communist Party. More than 58,000 Americans died fighting the forces he led. Saloth Sar, later known as Pol Pot, arrived in France on a scholarship in 1949 and joined the French Communist Party.

Then came Michel Foucault, whose argument that knowledge is an instrument of power swept American universities from the late 1970s and became a foundation of identity politics and critical race theory. In 1977 he signed an open letter urging France to abolish age-of-consent laws.

In 1978 Foucault reported from Iran hailing the uprising against the shah as a “political spirituality.” Months later, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini flew home from exile outside Paris on a chartered Air France plane arranged, according to a French diplomat, by the French government. In November 1979, Khomeini’s followers seized the U.S. Embassy in Tehran and seized American hostages, 52 of whom it held for 444 days.

More recent French exports are economic. Thomas Piketty’s “Capital in the Twenty-First Century” proposed a global progressive wealth tax. In 2019 his collaborators Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman designed Sen. Elizabeth Warren’s proposed wealth tax. In France the “Zucman tax,” 2% a year on fortunes above €100 million, initially passed the National Assembly in 2025 before the French Senate rejected it.

The idea has migrated to California, where voters soon will cast ballots on Proposition 40, which Mr. Saez helped design. This tax would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires, counting anyone who lived in the state on Jan. 1, 2026—10 months before the vote.

Proponents promise $100 billion in revenue, but Hoover Institution economists estimate closer to $30 billion. Once forgone income-tax revenue is counted, the tax could leave California about $39 billion worse off.

France shows where the road ends, having already run this experiment. It taxed wealth for most of the period 1982-2017, when President Emmanuel Macron scrapped the levy and replaced it with a narrower tax on real estate. By then the wealth tax raised only about €5 billion a year while its payers kept leaving. In 2016 alone, France lost a net 550 wealthy households.

Decades of faith in the state have pushed public spending above 57% of gross domestic product. Soviet government spending in 1999 was only 50%. French public debt stands near €3.5 trillion, or 119% of GDP, and this month French 10-year bond yields crossed 5% for the first time since 2002 and are above those of Portugal, Italy, Greece and Spain.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the hard left, is polling second for next April’s presidential election. He proposes to take the roughly 18% of French bonds held by the Bank of France and, in his words, “chuck it in the fire”—a solution likely to lead to another financial crisis.

The barricades have returned too. Student protests over school funding and the cost of living have turned violent. The approximately 15-basis-point increase in French bond yields following the civil unrest will ultimately add another €5.4 billion in interest expenses to the already strained French budget.

The Statue of Liberty turns 140 this week and remains a gift worth keeping. Some of the other gifts should be returned to sender.

Everyone knows I don’t care much for the old Latin Mass and that I am fond of defending and promoting the Novus Ordo, but that being said, I think the approach of the Church to the TLM crowd is inconsistent with our broader ecumenical theology, inconsistent with our embrace of liturgical diversity and our even permitting theological diversity, inconsistent with the existence of the Anglican Ordinariate, and with our offers to re-unite with the Orthodox without requiring them to accept Vatican 1, etc. 

If I were Pope I would spend a lot of time showing the deficiencies in the old Latin Mass and the superiority and treasures of the Novus Ordo, but I don’t think I would prohibit parishes which have a majority of lay people asking for the TLM from celebrating it. Perhaps I would require that priests make sure that the congregation understands Latin, or something like that. But an outright prohibition, I can’t really square with everything else. 

This is where the need to fully implement Vatican II comes in. Paradoxically perhaps, the full implementation involves an ecumenism and a synodality and a liberty that allows even for more traditional forms of faith and worship, so long as those forms aren’t hostile to the Church.

text:
Ephesians 3:14 Commentary
1. Verse Quoted in KJV
“For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” Ephesians 3:14
2. Detailed Exegesis of Each Natural Phrase
“For this cause”
Paul begins, “For this cause,” and those words reach backward into the tremendous doctrinal ground he has just covered. The expression first appeared in Ephesians 3:1: “For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles.” Paul then interrupted the sentence to explain the mystery, his stewardship of grace, the one body, the unsearchable riches of Christ, the manifold wisdom of God, and the eternal purpose accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord. After warning the Ephesians not to faint at his tribulations, he returns to the prayer he was beginning earlier. Doctrine has brought him to his knees. He has not studied the mystery merely so he can draw a better chart; what God has revealed moves him to pray that believers actually experience the spiritual strength appropriate to their position.
That is one of the great lessons of the verse. Biblical doctrine should lead to prayer, worship, holiness, and spiritual dependence. If a man can spend years learning Scripture and become harder, colder, prouder, and less prayerful, he has learned information without allowing truth to govern him. Paul has just written about things hidden from ages, heavenly principalities, God’s eternal purpose, and direct access through Christ. His response is not to congratulate himself on being the man who knows these truths. He bows. The man who has genuinely seen something of God’s eternal purpose usually discovers that knees are more useful than applause.
“For this cause” also means Paul’s prayer is rooted in objective truth rather than emotional impulse. He is not praying because the Ephesians happen to be having a bad week. He is praying because of what God has made them in Christ. They are fellowheirs. They are of the same body. They possess access with confidence. They are part of the Church through which God displays His wisdom. Paul therefore asks God to make the inward life of these believers correspond more fully with their exalted spiritual position. Christian prayer is strongest when it grows from doctrine. The best prayers are not attempts to talk God into becoming faithful; they are responses to what His word has already declared Him to be.
“I bow my knees”
Paul says, “I bow my knees.” Scripture records prayer in more than one bodily posture, so the verse should not be turned into a legalistic rule claiming that every legitimate prayer must be offered on the knees. Abraham stood before the LORD in Genesis 18:22. David sat before the LORD in 2 Samuel 7:18. Jesus spoke of men standing and praying in Mark 11:25. Yet kneeling is a deeply biblical expression of humility, submission, worship, and earnestness. Solomon “kneeled down upon his knees” when dedicating the temple (2 Chronicles 6:13). Daniel “kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed” (Daniel 6:10). Jesus Himself “kneeled down, and prayed” in Luke 22:41.
Paul’s posture therefore fits the burden of the prayer. He is a prisoner, but the Roman chains have not prevented him from entering the presence of God. Rome may control where his body is housed, but it cannot control where his prayer goes. The man who has just told the Ephesians not to faint now demonstrates where spiritual endurance is found. He bends before God rather than bending before circumstances. The world often interprets kneeling as weakness, but Scripture presents it as a position from which believers can stand spiritually. A man on his knees before God may be standing taller than an empire that thinks it has him chained.
The expression also exposes the foolishness of spiritual pride. Paul has received tremendous revelation, yet revelation has not made him self-sufficient. He does not say, “I have sufficient doctrine now; prayer is unnecessary.” Knowledge sends him lower. First Corinthians 8:1

text:
550 people. One Monday. Zero phone calls. 

Imagine this. You wake up, log in, mark your attendance, and start your work like any other day. You're training the AI the whole world calls  the future.

By lunch, your laptop logs you out. Then your ID stops working. Then your colleague's. Then the person next to them. By evening, a WhatsApp group of nearly 500 strangers is asking the same question: You too?

There was no HR call, no meeting, and no goodbye. You find out from an email sent to your personal inbox, because your work email doesn't exist anymore. You open the HR portal and your payslip is already generated: Last working day: today. You can't even download it, because payroll access was the first thing they cut.

The reason they gave was ramp-down of the business assignment. It wasn't your performance and it wasn't your fault. One big client pulled back, and roughly 550 Indian families reportedly paid the price in a single day.

Your final settlement is ready, but you'll only get it after you return the company laptop. They took your access in minutes. They'll return your money on their terms.

Then the market spoke. Innodata stock crashed 26% the next day, because investors realised what employees learned the hard way: • fewer projects means less revenue • 58% of revenue reportedly depends on ONE client • leadership has offered zero transparency

So yes, I'm glad the stock fell. Nobody wins here, but for once, treating human beings like disposable logins came with a price tag.
To the 550: you built the data behind AI that billions of people will use. You deserved dignity. You deserved a phone call, at the very least.
Companies remember quarterly results. People remember how you let them go.

text:
Payments chains charge very little fees and operate on razor thing margins, because they offer a service that has been commoditized. If trying to optimize Zcash to be a payments chain like Temple you either lose to undercutting if fees or your fees get too low to be sustainable. Filling up blockspace with $0.00001 transactions would essentially be a DDoS on Zcash.

SoV does not mean *no transactions*, it just does not have the velocity of the last mile payments currency. But the transactions are important and worth paying a premium for, because of the scarce asset.

But yes, we need to scale the chain to have a higher transaction velocity! Currently the chain can process 2.9 transactions per second, and there are people working on 10xing that every 6 months to about 50k per second.

Still, the point of ZEC is both protection from fiat devaluation and surveillance. It is not currently designed to be a last mile payments chain, nor would it have any competitive advantage by attacking that market as a first move.

The whole point of the emissions curve is to bootstrap the Store of Value > Medium of Exchange > Unit of Account evolution over time, while keeping the chain secure.

The clock is certainly ticking to get Zcash more widely distributed as a store of value and move things towards low-to-medium velocity medium of exchange, and eventually Zcash as digital cash is realized.

Jumping right into "be a stablecoin" is not the answer for ZEC.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
In September 1978 Mary Vincent was a 15-year-old runaway hitchhiking to her grandfather's house when a 51-year-old man pulled over and offered her a ride.

He drove her down a deserted road, attacked her, and then picked up a hatchet and cut off both of her arms. He threw her into a ravine and said, "You want to be set free? I'll set you free," and drove away thinking she would bleed to death there.

She packed what was left of her arms with dirt to slow the bleeding, climbed a 30-foot embankment with no hands and stumbled to the road until a car finally stopped for her.

In the video below Mary, now a grown woman, talks about what was going through her head down in that ravine, and it wasn't fear for herself.

"He's going to do this to somebody else. I can't let that happen."

From her hospital bed she helped a sketch artist draw his face. At the trial she stood up, raised the hook where her hand used to be and pointed it at Lawrence Singleton.

He got 14 years, the most California allowed back then, and served 8. When he walked out in 1987, towns protested and nobody wanted him living near them.

Ten years later in Florida he killed a 31-year-old mother named Roxanne Hayes.

Mary is a mother of two now, and California changed the law because of her. But the man who cut off a child's arms was free again before she even turned 25. Can 8 years ever be enough for something like that?

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

Gold Movie

Gold is a 2016 American epic crime drama film directed by Stephen Gaghan and written by Patrick Massett and John Zinman. The film stars Matthew McConaughey, Édgar Ramírez, Bryce Dallas Howard, Corey Stoll, Toby Kebbell, Craig T. Nelson, Stacy Keach and Bruce Greenwood. The film is loosely based on the true story of the 1997 Bre-X mining scandal, when a massive gold deposit was supposedly discovered in the jungles of Indonesia; however, for legal reasons and to enhance the appeal of the film, character names and story details were changed.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
This bird has zero pink in it.

Not a drop. Not one molecule of red, magenta, or violet pigment anywhere on its body.

Grind that feather into powder and you get dust the color of a burnt match.

And yet, at the right angle, it outshines a brake light.

Nature has been running one trick for tens of millions of years. Engineers, banks, and fashion labs are now trying to copy it. And almost nobody knows that the color you see is not a color at all.

It's an event.

Read this slowly. By the end, you will never look at color the same way.

We'll cover the nano-machine in the feather, a dive that beats a fighter pilot's blackout limit, a tongue that fooled science for a century, and a nightly shutdown that looks exactly like death.

All in a body the weight of a nickel.

—

1. THE BIGGEST LIE YOUR EYES TELL YOU

Quick test. What color is a red apple?

You said red. Wrong question.

An apple contains molecules that swallow most of the light and throw back the red part. The color lives in the chemistry. Pigment. Dye. Paint. Take the molecule away and the color dies.

That's the system you were taught. It runs on about 99% of the objects you've ever touched.

But there is a second system. It's older, stranger, and far more violent in its beauty.

It uses no pigment at all.

It's called structural color. The color is not stored in a molecule. It's built out of geometry. Layers so thin that light itself gets confused and starts fighting with itself.

Soap bubbles do it. Oil on a wet road does it. The back of a CD does it. Opal does it.

But nothing, nothing, does it like a hummingbird.

—

2. THE FEATHER IS NOT A FEATHER. IT'S A MACHINE.

Zoom into the throat of a male Anna's hummingbird and the first surprise is how ordinary the raw materials are.

Keratin. The same protein as your fingernails.

Melanin. The same pigment that makes human hair dark and freckles brown. Brown. Black. The most boring pigment on Earth.

Air. Plain air.

That's the whole parts list. Nothing exotic. Nothing glowing. Nothing rare.

What changes everything is how those three ingredients are arranged.

Each tiny feather barb carries even tinier branches called barbules. Inside those barbules, the bird stacks flat, microscopic plates of melanin, and each plate is packed with trapped air bubbles.

Stack after stack after stack. Plate, air, plate, air, plate, air.

Each layer is only a few hundred nanometers thick. A human hair is about 70,000 nanometers wide. We are building with slices more than 100 times thinner than a hair.

And the spacing is not random. It is tuned to the wavelength of visible light, which runs from roughly 400 to 700 nanometers.

The bird isn't coloring its feathers.

It's building a microscopic optical instrument out of pigment that is brown, and getting fire.

—

3. WHY BROWN PLUS AIR EQUALS FIRE

Here is what happens when a ray of light lands on that stack.

Part of it bounces off the top layer. Part of it passes through and bounces off the second layer. Part goes deeper and bounces off the third. Dozens of tiny reflections come back out, one after another, each slightly delayed from the last.

Now the key. Light is a wave.

If two returning waves are perfectly in step, crest meets crest, they add together and the color gets louder. If they are out of step, crest meets trough, they cancel and the color vanishes.

The spacing of the layers decides which colors survive and which are erased.

Layers a certain thickness: the red waves line up, and everything else gets destroyed.

Slightly thinner: green survives.

Thinner again: blue.

That's it. That's the entire secret. Not chemistry. Arithmetic with light.

And there is a reason the effect is so intense. Melanin bends light hard. Air barely bends it at all. The contrast between the two is enormous, and the bigger the contrast between neighboring layers, the more light gets thrown back at each boundary.

Evolution accidentally discovered one of the most efficient reflective stacks in biology and then put it on a creature the weight of a nickel.

—

4. THE FEATHER THAT TURNS OFF

Here's where it gets creepy.

Rotate that feather a few degrees, and the color changes. Rotate it a few more, and the flame goes out completely. Not dimmer. Gone. Black.

Same feather. Same bird. Same light. Different angle.

Why? Because the path light takes through the layers changes with the angle. The timing between the reflected waves shifts, the in-step waves fall out of step, and the color is erased.

This is the part most people miss: the red isn't on the bird.

The red exists only in a narrow cone of space between the feather and your eye. Step outside that cone and it doesn't exist. Move your head and you are not seeing the same feather. You are seeing a different one that has just turned dark.

Pigment is a property of the object.

Structural color is a property of the relationship between the object, the light, and you.

Which means that every hummingbird flash you have ever seen was a private show. Meant for exactly one viewer standing exactly there.

—

5. A MAN WHO BUILT NUCLEAR PLANTS TOOK THE FIRST GOOD PICTURES

In the mid-20th century, one of the most obsessive hummingbird researchers on the planet was not a biologist.

Crawford Greenewalt was the president of DuPont. The same company that scaled up nylon and ran the industrial machinery behind the Manhattan Project. A man whose job involved millions of dollars and very serious chemistry.

His hobby: freezing hummingbirds in midair.

He worked with high-speed flash engineering, the kind of stroboscopic technology pioneered at MIT, to capture wings that beat dozens of times a second. His book *Hummingbirds*, published in 1960, became a landmark. And his era of research helped establish that those colors weren't chemical.

The classic test is simple and brutal.

Soak a feather in a liquid that fills the tiny air pockets and removes the optical contrast between the layers. The structure stops working.

The brilliant color drops away.

The pigment was never the source. Take the air out, and the fire goes out with it.

That is one of the cleanest experiments in all of biology: delete one invisible ingredient and watch the miracle die.

—

6. WHAT THE COLOR IS ACTUALLY FOR

Let's be honest about why this exists.

It's not for you. It's not for beauty. It's an advertisement with a very specific audience.

The male Anna's hummingbird is a tiny territorial warrior. He defends his patch of flowers like a nightclub bouncer. He needs rivals to back off and females to pay attention.

So he developed a signal that can be switched on and off.

Face the rival head-on, tilt the throat toward the sun, and the gorget ignites. Turn away and it goes dark. A flicker of color that can read like a warning shot, a flirt, or a threat, depending on who is watching.

You cannot do this with pigment. Pigment is always on. It's a billboard.

Structural color is a signal that can be aimed. A laser pointer made of feathers.

And the Anna's hummingbird has a detail that sets it apart from most of its relatives: the iridescence is not limited to the throat. It spreads up over the crown of the head. A hood of living light.

That's the species. Now here's what he does with it.

—

7. THE MOVE THAT SHOULDN'T BE POSSIBLE

During courtship, the male does this.

He climbs. Thirty meters or more, roughly the height of a ten-story building, straight up, until he is a dot.

Then he folds, and he drops.

Researchers at UC Berkeley clocked the dive at around 27 meters per second. That's about 60 miles per hour.

For a bird four inches long.

Scale it to body size and the number stops making sense. The dive works out to roughly 385 body lengths per second.

For reference:

A peregrine falcon, the animal everyone uses as the speed symbol, tops out near 200 body lengths per second in its dive.

A space shuttle reentering the atmosphere clocks around 207.

By this measure, the tiny bird with the pink hood is faster than all of them. Reported as the fastest vertebrate on Earth relative to its size.

And then comes the part that should terrify any pilot.

At the bottom of the dive, he pulls out of it. The turn puts around 9 g on his body. Trained fighter pilots in a g-suit start to gray out around that level.

And he does it in a heartbeat. Then does it again. And again. For a mate.

—

8. THE SOUND THAT ISN'T A VOICE

At the very bottom of the dive, there's a sharp, high-pitched chirp.

For years, people assumed it was the bird singing.

It isn't.

In 2008, researcher Christopher Clark tested it, and the answer was stranger. The sound is not from the throat. It's made by the tail.

As he flares at the bottom, the outer tail feathers flutter in the airflow like a reed in a wind instrument, and they produce the note.

A tiny wind instrument built into the tail. Played at 60 mph. For an audience of one.

So the full performance is this:

A climb. A dive. A flash of structural fire aimed at the female at exactly the right angle, a chirp made by feathers, and a 9 g pullout.

All in about a second.

Nobody taught him. No rehearsal. No coach. The whole routine is encoded in a creature whose brain weighs less than a paperclip.

—

9. THE ENGINE INSIDE

All of this runs on a power plant that should not work.

A hummingbird's heart can beat more than 1,200 times per minute in flight. That's about 20 beats every second.

Its wings beat around 50 times per second.

Its metabolism is the highest of any warm-blooded animal relative to size. The fuel is nectar, basically sugar water, and the bird needs roughly its own body weight in it, or more, every day.

Scale that to a human and you would need to eat the equivalent of thousands of burgers daily or your body temperature would climb past anything survivable.

And nectar burns fast. Flying is so expensive that a hummingbird that does not feed for a few hours can be in real trouble.

Which brings up a problem.

How does an animal that burns this hot survive the night?

—

10. THE OFF SWITCH

It shuts itself down.

Every night, many hummingbirds enter a state called torpor. It's like hibernation, but nightly.

The heart rate drops from over a thousand beats per minute to as low as about 50.

Body temperature falls from around 40°C into the teens or lower.

Breathing nearly stops. The bird hangs there, stiff, cold, unresponsive, often mistaken for dead by people who find one.

And in the morning, it wakes up. Reheats. Starts again.

Think about this for a second. The creature with the highest-voltage lifestyle in the animal kingdom can also, on command, nearly power itself off, and come back.

The same body that does a 9 g dive is the one that can fall into a coma every night to survive until sunrise.

—

11. THE TONGUE THAT BROKE A 100-YEAR-OLD THEORY

For a century, textbooks said hummingbirds drink by capillary action. The tongue is a tube. Nectar climbs up it like water in a straw.

In 2011, a biologist named Alejandro Rico-Guevara put high-speed cameras on feeding hummingbirds and watched what the tongue actually does.

The textbook was wrong.

The tip of the tongue splits in two. The edges are lined with tiny flaps. When the tongue hits nectar, the flaps spring open and trap the liquid. Then they zip shut as the tongue pulls back in.

A pump. A trap. A microscopic mechanism that fires about 15 times per second.

The reason it took 100 years to find out: nobody had a camera fast enough to see it.

Hold that thought. It's the theme of this entire story.

—

12. YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE BUDGET VERSION

Now the part that should bother you.

Humans have three types of color sensors in the eye. Red, green, blue. Everything you've ever seen is built from mixing those three.

Hummingbirds have four.

Their fourth cone is tuned into ultraviolet, a range of light that is entirely invisible to us.

In 2020, researchers published work showing hummingbirds don't just see UV. They can tell apart combinations of colors that don't exist in the rainbow, mixes like UV plus green or UV plus red. Colors for which humans have no name, and cannot imagine.

The study stated it flatly: hummingbirds see colors we can't.

Which means that when you look at that gorget, you aren't seeing what the female sees.

You're seeing a compressed version. A low-resolution preview.

Somewhere in that flash is information that was written for an eye you don't have.

The most spectacular thing in the frame might be the part you can't see.

—

13. THE ARMS RACE NOBODY TALKS ABOUT

Why would evolution do something this expensive?

Building nanoscale layers of precise thickness inside a living feather, inside a bird that grows them from scratch, in a pattern that cannot be off by more than a few percent, is expensive. Accurate. Fragile.

Darwin hated it.

When he thought about peacock feathers, which use a related structural trick, he wrote to a friend that the sight of a feather in the tail of a peacock made him sick.

Not because it was ugly. Because it was a problem.

Natural selection said: survive. Be efficient. Stay hidden.

And here was a bird putting its energy into a glowing, tail-dragging, predator-attracting display.

His answer, which became one of the most debated ideas in biology: sometimes survival isn't the only pressure. Sometimes being chosen is.

A female picks the male whose color is brightest. The brightest color requires the most precisely built structure. The most precise structure signals a healthy, well-fed, capable body.

Beauty as a lie detector. The signal is expensive precisely because it's hard to fake.

Which is a surprisingly modern idea: the best proof of quality is something that costs a lot to produce.

—

14. NOW HUMANS WANT IT BACK

Here's where the story leaves the garden.

Because structural color has three properties that every engineer dreams about.

One. It doesn't fade. Pigments break down in sunlight. They bleach. A structure does not. As long as the geometry survives, the color survives.

Two. It uses no dye. The textile industry is routinely cited as one of the largest sources of industrial water pollution on the planet. A color without dye means a color without toxic runoff.

Three. It can be tuned. Change the spacing and you change the color, with no new chemicals.

And people are already using it.

Banknotes. Look at the numeral on a high-value note. The one that shifts from one color to another when you tilt it. That's a thin-film interference trick, the same physics in the throat of a hummingbird, protecting billions of dollars from forgers. A criminal can copy a pigment. It's much harder to copy a nanostructure.

Fabric. A Japanese company, Teijin, developed a fiber called Morphotex, inspired by the Morpho butterfly, which makes color through layered structures rather than dye.

Screens. Qualcomm built a display technology called Mirasol, which borrowed from the same butterfly principle, and reflected ambient light rather than burning battery to emit it.

Berries. A tropical plant called Pollia, with a small blue fruit, has one of the most intense structural colors measured in any living thing. Researchers in Cambridge found it's made not of pigment but of tiny twisted cellulose fibers, the same stuff in cotton and paper. A common plant fiber, arranged into one of the brightest colors ever measured in nature.

Cosmetics, paints, car finishes, sensors, solar technology: all of it is in labs right now.

The funniest part?

The best engineers in the world, with millions in funding and billion-dollar fabrication plants, are still trying to match a four-gram bird that builds the same thing at room temperature, out of its own body, in a few weeks.

—

15. 15. THE BLUE LIE

Here's a fact that sounds fake.

Almost no bird on Earth has blue pigment.

A blue jay. A bluebird. A kingfisher. A peacock's neck. None of them contain a drop of blue dye.

Their blue is built the same way: tiny structures inside the feather that scatter short wavelengths and throw them back at your eye.

Crush a blue jay feather and the blue disappears. The powder turns brown.

Think about how strange that is. The color you associate most with calm, sky, and trust, in the entire bird kingdom, is a trick of nanoscale architecture.

The sky itself is a version of the same trick. Air molecules scatter blue light more than red. Nothing in the atmosphere is blue either.

The most familiar color in the world is mostly an effect. Not an ingredient.

—

16. THE WEIRDEST VERSIONS OF THE TRICK

Once you know the rule, you start seeing it everywhere. And it gets bizarre.

The whitest beetle. A beetle in Southeast Asia, in the genus Cyphochilus, is white to a degree that outperforms most manufactured white materials. Its scales are only about five micrometers thick, and the pigment inside them is nothing. Just a tangled network of chitin that scatters light so efficiently that almost none of it escapes. A thinner coat than paper, and brighter than paper.

The beetle that talks in spirals. Certain scarab beetles reflect light that is circularly polarized, twisting left, a property almost nothing else in nature produces. Most animals can't even detect it. Some beetles can. A hidden channel of communication, in plain sight, invisible to nearly everything including you.

The butterfly that breaks glass rules. The Morpho butterfly's wings look electric blue from far away. Under a microscope they carry rows of tiny ridges shaped like Christmas trees. Each ridge is a stack of layers. Rotate the wing and it flickers like a signal lamp, visible from hundreds of meters in a forest.

Peacocks. Those eyes in the tail are built from microscopic rods in a repeating grid. A photonic crystal. Change the spacing of the grid slightly, and the color goes from blue to green to yellow to brown, all with the same material.

And then the hummingbird. The champion. Because it combines the highest brilliance, the sharpest angle control, and the richest color range in a surface thinner than a hair.

Evolution did this independently, many separate times, in birds, beetles, butterflies, plants, and even deep-sea animals. When the same invention appears over and over from separate starting points, it usually means one thing:

It's not a quirk. It's a solution.

—

17. THE COLOR THAT RENEWS ITSELF

Here's the engineering problem nobody mentions.

A feather is dead tissue. Once it's grown, the bird can't repair it. It can't repaint it. It can't patch a scratch.

If the structure gets damaged, the color is simply gone.

So the bird does the only thing it can: it replaces the entire surface. Feathers molt on a schedule, and fresh nanostructures grow in, built from scratch, with the same precision, using the same instructions.

Think about the manufacturing challenge. A new optical device, tuned to hundreds of nanometers, assembled by cells, without a clean room, without a microscope, without a blueprint anyone can see.

The blueprint is in the DNA. The factory is a follicle. The product is a feather whose accuracy would make a semiconductor engineer nervous.

And it works. Every year. In wind, rain, and dust.

—

18. THE SPECIES THAT SHOULDN'T HAVE WON

One more detail about this particular bird, because it makes the whole story better.

A little over a century ago, the Anna's hummingbird was a bird of a narrow strip of California. Today you can find it up the Pacific coast, into British Columbia, and east into the desert Southwest.

It moved.

Gardens. Flowering exotic plants. Backyard feeders. People accidentally built it a buffet, and it took the offer.

It also does something almost no other hummingbird in its range does: it stays through the winter, in places that get cold, surviving on nectar, tiny insects, and the nightly shutdown described above.

So the creature with the most delicate optics in the bird world is also one of the toughest.

Elegance and ruthlessness, in four grams.

—

19. THREE EXPERIMENTS YOU CAN RUN TODAY

You don't need a lab. You need ten minutes.

One. Take any CD or DVD, or the back of a cheap holographic sticker. Tilt it under a lamp. Watch the colors sweep from one end of the rainbow to the other. No pigment. Just the spacing of microscopic grooves doing the same job as the stacks in a feather.

Two. Blow a soap bubble, or find oil on a puddle. The swirling colors change as the film thins. The same layer thickness tuning, the same waves canceling and reinforcing. Slower. Bigger. Easier to see.

Three. Hold a dark blue or iridescent feather, or a piece of shiny packaging, against the light. Move it slowly. Notice the exact moment the color vanishes. That is the moment the geometry falls out of tune.

That tiny vanishing is the whole principle. Everything in this post is that vanishing, scaled up, refined, and put on a bird.

—

20. THE WORLD RUNS SLOWER FOR THEM

One more thing, and it's the one that will stay in your head tonight.

Humans stop seeing flicker at around 60 flashes per second. Faster than that, and a flickering light looks steady. It's why a screen feels smooth to us.

Many birds can see flicker at rates well beyond that. Some measurements push far above what we can detect. To an animal like this, a normal screen can look like a strobe, and the world can have a finer time resolution than the one you live in.

Think about what that means for a creature whose wings beat 50 times a second, who dives at 60 mph, who must judge a flower's position, a rival's angle, and a mate's attention in fractions of a second.

For us, the dive is a blur. For them, it may be a sequence of clear frames.

We think of ourselves as the observers of nature. But there's a version of this where the bird is the one watching the slow-motion replay of us.

—

21. THE NUMBERS THAT SHOULDN'T FIT IN ONE ANIMAL

Let's put it together.

Weight: about the same as a nickel.

Heart: over 1,200 beats a minute.

Wings: about 50 beats a second.

Dive: 385 body lengths per second.

Force: roughly 9 g at pullout.

Tongue: about 15 licks per second, using a trap nobody saw for a century.

Night mode: heart rate from 1,000+ down to ~50.

Vision: a fourth color channel humans don't have.

Color: zero pigment. Pure geometry.

All in a creature that fits in the palm of your hand and that you will probably never notice.

—

22. THE PART THAT STAYS WITH YOU

There is a quiet lesson underneath all of this.

For most of human history, we believed color was a substance. Something you could grind, mix, and paint.

Then we found out the brightest thing in the natural world isn't a substance at all.

It's an arrangement.

Same atoms. Same boring brown melanin. Same air. Rearranged, and you get a glowing crown on a bird.

That's the idea worth taking out of this post.

Most of what makes something extraordinary isn't what it's made of.

It's how it's put together.

—

So the next time you see something shining, and you can't find the source of the glow, remember the bird with no pink in it.

Sometimes the most vivid thing in the world is an illusion built by exactly the right nothing.

If this changed how you see color, repost it. Someone you know thinks they understand light.

And follow for more: the hidden machinery inside ordinary things.

Pigment fades. Geometry doesn't. Remember that, and you'll start noticing the shine in everything.

—

P.S. A question, because I genuinely want to know.

If the most intense color in nature is made of brown, air, and good timing, what else around you is secretly the same kind of illusion?

The blue of the sky. The shine of a pearl. The shimmer on a beetle's back. The flash on a dragonfly in July.

Reply with the strangest example of structural color you've ever seen. I'll read every one, and the best will go in the next post.

Because the real hook of this whole story isn't a bird.

It's the moment you realize you've been looking at geometry your entire life and calling it color.

Repost if it landed.
