text:
What you see may feel continuous, but a new study in monkeys suggests the brain could be processing competing images in rapid turns.

Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley used a visual technique called flash suppression, in which a face shown to one eye is pushed out of awareness when another face is flashed to the other eye.

While recording brain activity in two macaque monkeys, the team found that signals associated with the visible and hidden faces appeared to alternate. 

Each state lasted around 60 milliseconds, with activity switching roughly 15 times a second.

The findings may offer clues about how timing relates to visual awareness. However, the study has not yet been peer reviewed, and it remains unclear what the monkeys consciously saw or whether the same process occurs in humans.

📜 THIS DAY IN DIPLOMATIC HISTORY
       October 28, 1962

On the morning of October 28, 1962, Radio Moscow read out a message from Nikita Khrushchev. The Soviet missiles in Cuba would be dismantled and shipped home. With that, the thirteen days in which the world came nearer to nuclear war than ever before or since came to an end. 

The roots were simple. After the failed, American-backed invasion of Cuba at the Bay of Pigs in 1961, Fidel Castro looked to Moscow for protection. And the United States had ringed the Soviet Union with nuclear missiles, among them Jupiter rockets in Turkey and Italy that could reach Soviet cities within minutes. In 1962 гnder the cover name Operation Anadyr, Khrushchev secretly shipped nuclear missiles to Cuba, both to shield the island and to narrow the gap with American power. On October 14 an American U-2 spy plane photographed the launch sites being built.

On October 22 President John Kennedy went on television, revealed the missiles, and declared a naval "quarantine" of Cuba. The word was chosen with care, because "blockade" meant an act of war. He also wrote to Khrushchev, demanding that the weapons be withdrawn. On October 25 the confrontation reached the floor of the UN, where the American envoy Adlai Stevenson demanded that the Soviet ambassador say yes or no to the missiles, and declared that he was prepared to wait for his answer "until hell freezes over."

The real turn came by correspondence. On the evening of October 26 Khrushchev sent a long and emotional letter. The two sides, he wrote, were pulling on the ends of a rope with the knot of war tied in the middle, and the harder each pulled, the tighter the knot would draw, until it might be bound so fast that even the man who had tied it could not undo it. Let us not pull, he urged, but take measures to untie that knot. His offer was plain: the Soviet Union would remove the missiles if the United States promised not to invade Cuba.

Then, on the morning of October 27, a second letter came, broadcast this time over Radio Moscow and markedly harder. It added a new price. The United States must also pull its Jupiter missiles out of Turkey.

That same day, October 27, everything nearly came apart. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba and its pilot, Major Rudolf Anderson, was killed, the only man to die in combat during the crisis. Another American plane strayed into Soviet airspace. Kennedy's generals pressed hard for air strikes and invasion.

Kennedy answered the warmer first letter and simply ignored the second, accepting the trade of withdrawal for a promise not to invade as though the demand over Turkey had never been made. Then, through a secret channel, he quietly met the harder price as well. That evening his brother, Attorney General Robert Kennedy, called in the Soviet ambassador, Anatoly Dobrynin, and gave him a private assurance. The United States would take its Jupiters out of Turkey within a few months, but this could never be made public or tied openly to the bargain.

Khrushchev took the offer. Fearing that events were slipping beyond anyone's control, he announced the withdrawal quickly and openly on October 28, before some new accident could undo it. The world breathed again.

In public it looked like a clean Soviet retreat, for the secret concession over Turkey stayed hidden for decades. The quarantine was lifted on November 20, 1962. The Jupiters left Turkey the following spring, just as promised. And within a year the two governments acted to make sure they would never again drift so near to disaster through slow and garbled messages. In 1963 they strung a direct teletype "hotline" between the Kremlin and the White House, and that August they signed the first treaty banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere. The crisis that had almost ended the world became the beginning of arms control.

text:
Port Houston’s September rebound was not evenly spread: container volume rose 11% year over year to 376,419 TEUs, but loaded imports jumped 16% while loaded exports managed only 2%.

That imbalance matters operationally. Import-heavy growth can pull more boxes, trucks and warehouse capacity into the Gulf gateway before export demand fully catches up. The 31% increase in empty-container exports—55,963 TEUs—also points to carriers repositioning equipment rather than simply moving more balanced two-way cargo.

There are signs of broader momentum: vessel movements climbed 10% in September, barge movements 23%, and the port launched a container-and-reefer service. Officials said exports accelerated late in September and early October, but continued growth is still an expectation, not a booked result.

For shippers, Houston may offer more service options, yet the near-term planning question is whether inland capacity and equipment flows keep pace with the import surge.

***************************************
Yes, several remote or relatively harsh islands are currently listed for sale, though the private-island market is dominated by tropical Caribbean/Pacific properties marketed for luxury retreats or resorts. Options that better match the original post’s idea of “less habitable” or isolated locations (remote, cold, undeveloped, or wilderness) include these examples drawn from recent listings:

- **Hildasay Island** (Shetland, Scotland): About 267 acres (110 hectares), uninhabited on a permanent basis (historically had a small community), with two freshwater lochs, varied coastline, and Atlantic exposure. Accessible by boat from the Shetland Mainland with its own pier. Listed at offers over £350,000. It is secluded and windy rather than tropical paradise territory.[](<https://t.co/qhFHj9w7T2>)

- **Roper Island** (Hyde County, North Carolina, USA): Roughly 8,700 acres of swamp, marsh, pocosin, and coastal forest, described as remote with boat-only access, no roads or amenities, and limited development potential due to wetlands. Marketed as a hunter’s paradise with wildlife (bears, hogs, waterfowl). Asking around $5.8 million; a large contiguous tract but logistically challenging.[](<https://t.co/dbQcnUHyNs>)

- **Virgin Island** (Patagonian Archipelago, Chile): A large, previously undeveloped island (reports cite it as roughly seven times Manhattan’s size or ~11,000 acres in coverage discussions) with mountains, lagoons, lakes, extensive coastline, and wilderness. Marketed for its isolation and raw character; earlier listings referenced prices in the $35–54 million range. Access typically by boat or helicopter.[](<https://t.co/74I4Ykq3sL>)

Additional colder or seasonal options appear in Canada (Nova Scotia lake/coastal islands, often under $1–2 million and freehold, with winter limitations) and Tasmania (e.g., Ninth Island and others in the Furneaux Group, freehold and remote). Very cheap small islets exist in places like Nicaragua’s Isletas or Finnish/Canadian archipelagos (sometimes under $100,000), but these are typically tiny and seasonal.

Specialized brokers such as Vladi Private Islands and Private Islands Inc. list many properties worldwide (hundreds available at any time). Truly extreme “uninhabitable” territory is rarer on the open market; governments control many of the harshest spots (e.g., certain Arctic or remote Pacific atolls), and historical penal islands like Coiba (Panama) or Islas Marías (Mexico) were state-run operations, not private purchases.

**Practical notes**: Ownership of a private island does not automatically allow operating a labor camp, prison, or large-scale relocation facility. That would require national government approval, compliance with local and international laws (including human-rights standards), massive logistics for food/water/security/medical care, and environmental clearances. Most listed islands remain under the sovereignty and zoning rules of their host country. Prices, availability, and exact details change quickly—confirm directly with brokers or agents for current status.
***************************************

Tether Gold is a gold-backed digital token issued by TG Commodities, part of the Tether group.

Each XAUT represents ownership of one fine troy ounce of physical gold.

Three major markets:

Buying XAUT isn't the same as holding a gold bar in your own possession.

Redemption involves eligibility requirements and fees.

The issuer also retains administrative powers over the token contract.

XAUT offers digital access to gold.

It doesn't eliminate the risks of financial intermediaries.

Tether Gold has a straightforward investment thesis.

Own gold exposure without handling physical bullion.

Its strengths?

Physical backing.

Blockchain transferability.

Fractional ownership.

Integration with crypto trading markets.

But its biggest weakness is counterparty dependence.

Gold prices rise, tokenized commodity adoption expands, and XAUT maintains credible backing and liquid markets.

The bearish case?

Gold declines, secondary-market liquidity deteriorates, or concerns emerge around custody and redemption.

text:
TeamGym : un environnement pour la prise de décision en équipe par des agents d’IA disposant d’informations distribuées : https://t.co/1Nv92pwVdW

"arXiv:2610.37571v1 [https://t.co/gQRNwvACTl] 27 Oct 2026
TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information
Chanwoo ParkJaywoong JeongZachary WojtowiczYubin KimTaekyun LeeKaiqing ZhangAsuman OzdaglarMIT KAIST UT Austin University of Maryland⋆Equal contribution.Abstract
Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants. Yet AI agents are still primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation. We introduce TeamGym, an environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making problems constructed from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. TeamGym introduces a method to identify a minimal set of facts, each element of which is necessary and all of which are collectively sufficient for a correct final decision, which we call pivotal information. This enables TeamGym to both control the distribution of pivotal information and track how well agents identify and integrate pivotal information when making team decisions. Examining 8 language models on 12 source corpora, we find that current AI agents often fail to effectively share information: Distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average relative to giving the same information to a single model (a communication gap). We also document that participants do not effectively retrieve decision-relevant information on their own: A team’s success rate is lowered by a further 19.9 points when participants must identify and extract pivotal information from source material rather than receiving it directly (a retrieval gap). To help remedy these deficits, we use TeamGym to train policies through reinforcement learning on team decision loss. Across two policy-training experiments, we find that training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.Fig. 1:TeamGym overview. TeamGym distributes pivotal information across participants, structures evidence exchange during team interaction, and evaluates the resulting decision. Its controlled conditions separate communication and retrieval gaps, while the training loop supports configurable policy optimization.

1Introduction
The frontier of AI is turning to multi-agent systems, in which AI agents are organized into teams that communicate to solve problems (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026a). Yet AI models are still trained and benchmarked largely as individual agents, which raises the question of whether they acquire the capacities and dispositions needed to be effective teammates. In human groups, collective intelligence, which is linked to social sensitivity and turn-taking, predicts team performance better than individual intelligence (Woolley et al., 2010). Although AI agents differ from humans, this finding motivates evaluating them as teams rather than only as individuals.A central challenge in team decision-making is that decision-relevant information is typically distributed across members. Reaching a collective decision requires members to identify and retrieve relevant information, communicate it efficiently, and integrate it into a final decision. Team theory has long studied this challenge (Radner, 1962; Marschak and Radner, 1972), while empirical research on human group decision-making finds that people often struggle to identify and integrate critical private information (Stasser and Titus, 1985; Lu et al., 2012).We introduce TeamGym, a gym for constructing team decision problem instances from source corpora, and for evaluating and training participant and coordinator policies under controlled information distributions and communication structures. TeamGym targets questions that existing benchmarks and multi-agent systems leave open. Single-agent benchmarks measure individual model capabilities (Wu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024), while research on multi-agent LLM systems focuses on designing harnesses that solve a given problem (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026b). Neither offers much evidence on whether participants can retrieve and communicate decision-relevant information, how team performance varies with information distribution and communication structure, or whether training can improve participant and coordinator policies.
1.0.0.1 Method.
TeamGym constructs controlled team decision problem instances from real-world source corpora. For each instance, it derives a decision objective from one or more corpus questions and either retains a corpus-provided reference decision or constructs one from corpus annotations and source materials. Source annotations and reasoning associated with the reference decision guide the selection of candidate evidence units, such as sentences, paragraphs, tables, or code blocks. Source-specific grounding and model-based complete-set and leave-one-out checks retain units that together support the reference decision but whose individual removal leaves it unsupported or unresolved. These retained units are pivotal information units (PIUs) and collectively form the instance’s pivotal information.Holding the problem instance and its pivotal information fixed, TeamGym can vary who initially has each PIU (the PIU distribution), whether participants receive PIUs directly or source material containing them, the communication structure, and token budgets. The team collectively receives the pivotal information, but the evidence is distributed across participants to make communication necessary for a fully supported final decision. The communication structure specifies whether a coordinator controls communication, how speakers are selected, and which decision maker makes the final decision. Token budgets constrain what decision makers may observe and generate. To understand what reduces team performance, we define two success-rate gaps. The communication gap is the drop when the same PIUs are distributed across participants rather than given to one model. The retrieval gap is the further drop when the team must retrieve those PIUs from source material rather than receive them directly. Beyond evaluation, TeamGym supports training participant and coordinator policies under controlled PIU distributions, communication structures, and token budgets.Table 1:Source corpora and decisions. The problem instances constructed from the source corpora use different source materials and decision objectives across four domains.DomainSource corporaDecisionsLegalCUAD, MAUD, eCFR Casebook,MSLR, Multi-LexSum, SARAContract profiles, merger reviews, compliance and enforcement,legal and procedural conclusions, and tax calculationsFinanceFinDVer, FinLongDocQASEC-filing findings, calculations, comparisons, and classificationsMedicalMLCR, EvidenceBenchEvidence-grounded medical reviews and biomedical answersSoftwareengineeringSWE Atlas–Codebase QnA, DeepSWECodebase QA and multi-turn, long-horizon repository-levelcode repair with functionally evaluated patches
We construct problem instances from source corpora in Table 1 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023b; Office of the Federal Register, 2026a; Office of the Federal Register, 2026b; Yu et al., 2027; Shen et al., 2022; Holzenberger et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026; Wisedocs, 2026; Wang et al., 2025; Raghavendra et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). Source materials include contracts, regulations, SEC filings, biomedical papers, and source code, while the decision formats are finite-choice, written, and numeric.
1.0.0.2 Findings.
The resulting comparisons hold the problem instance and pivotal information fixed to isolate communication and retrieval effects from differences in problem difficulty. (1) Across eight language models and 12 source corpora, the decision success rate is 22.9 percentage points lower when the same PIUs are distributed across a team than when one model receives them all, and a further 19.9 points lower when the same team must retrieve its PIUs from source material rather than receiving them directly. (2) Across domains, differences in the success rate among communication structures vary across PIU-distribution conditions. For example, across the six legal source corpora when participants receive PIUs directly, sequential communication in which each speaker selects the next participant leads simultaneous communication by 3.9 points when one PIU is initially common to the team, but trails it by 9.8 points when the team includes an additional participant without a PIU, corresponding to a 13.8-point change in the difference between their success rates. (3) Optimizing final-decision quality changes the communication process itself. With coordinator control, joint two-policy training produces a compact, exhaustive information-elicitation protocol; without a coordinator, training the shared participant policy improves end-to-end final-decision quality and completion and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication. Tracing PIUs through these trajectories shows that increased participation makes more pivotal information available on FinDVer validation, but not on held-out FinLongDocQA.TeamGym therefore provides a controlled environment in which team decision-making capabilities can be evaluated and trained under different information distributions and communication structures.
2Related Work

2.0.0.1 Team decision theory and organizational economics.
Team decision theory studies cooperative decision makers with a team objective and a decentralized information structure. A team problem couples a shared objective with an information structure and one policy for each decision maker (Radner, 1962; Marschak and Radner, 1972; Yüksel and Başar, 2013). Classical analysis largely studies the properties of different computation structures and policies, not how they can be learned and implemented computationally. Under tractable joint-policy optimization (A1), computing this collection is assumed feasible before execution, although the exact problem can be intractable even in finite-horizon decentralized control (Bernstein et al., 2002). TeamGym instead evaluates and trains language-model policies, comparing policy collections before and after training under the same conditions.
2.0.0.2 Mechanism design.
Under the direct-report mechanism assumption (A2), mechanism design represents private information as a type that can be elicited directly under the applicable equilibrium assumptions, and that participants know their type and can communicate it if they so choose (Maskin and Sjostrom, 2002; Myerson, 1979; Myerson, 2008). In practice, however, attention and cognitive limitations constrain agent’s ability to identify, extract, and communicate information contained in long source material, even if it is in principle available to them (Mookherjee, 2006). TeamGym assumes a shared team payoff and studies bounded natural-language messages derived from source material.
2.0.0.3 Communication constraints.
Research in organizational economics, planning, and reinforcement learning examines communication costs and message limits (Cremer et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2024). The idealization of nonbinding communication resources (A3) permits decision makers to access and transmit relevant information without binding observation or message constraints. TeamGym instead makes its resource budgets explicit.We defer additional related work on multistage communication, human-AI and group decision making, multi-agent LLM systems, benchmark contrasts, and the source corpora to Section 6.
3TeamGym Environment

3.1Decision Problem and Communication
We formalize TeamGym as a finite-horizon team decision problem (Radner, 1962; Marschak and Radner, 1972; Yüksel and Başar, 2013; Nayyar et al., 2013). A problem instance q fixes underlying source materials, a decision objective, a decision format, a set 𝒟q of possible final decisions, and a problem-specific evaluator that assigns each d∈𝒟q a team payoff Uq​(d)∈[0,1]. A decision maker is a role whose policy may generate a query, send a message, or make the final decision. A participant is a decision maker that may send messages during communication. A coordinator is a decision maker that may control communication by selecting or querying participants and may make the final decision. Initially, each participant receives an initial local observation, while all decision makers receive the same initial common observation containing the decision objective and decision format. The policy ρi maps the information currently available to decision maker i to a distribution over the queries, messages, or final decisions permitted for its role; ρ denotes the collection of decision-maker policies. The communication structure 𝒞 specifies whether a coordinator controls communication, which participants may send messages and when, whether messages are sequential or simultaneous, and which decision maker makes the final decision. The resource budgets B, including token budgets, constrain what decision makers may observe and generate and how often participants may send messages. Queries and messages form the communication transcript; a decision maker’s local transcript is the portion available to it under 𝒞 and B. The initial local and common observations, together with the observation rules induced by 𝒞 and the observation limits in B, define the decentralized information structure. An episode is one complete execution through the final-decision stage for fixed q, initial observations, 𝒞, B, and ρ. For these fixed inputs, the resulting interaction induces a distribution over final decisions, and we evaluate ρ by its expected team payoff, 𝔼​[Uq​(d)]. Holding q and the initial observations fixed while varying 𝒞, B, or ρ changes the interaction conditions without changing the problem instance.For evaluation, we consider five communication structures (Figure 2), each proceeding in scheduled steps called communication rounds: (1) Round robin, under which one participant sends a message per round in a fixed cyclic order; (2) Current-speaker selection, which starts with the first participant in that order, after which each speaker selects the next participant; (3) Simultaneous responses, under which all participants respond in one round; (4) Coordinator-selected speaker, under which the coordinator selects and queries one participant per round; and (5) Broadcast query, under which the coordinator sends the same query to all participants, whose responses are generated in the same round. In Round robin, Current-speaker selection, and Simultaneous responses, no coordinator controls communication, and a separate final decision maker that does not participate in communication reads the complete communication transcript and makes the final decision. In Coordinator-selected speaker and Broadcast query, the coordinator controls communication and makes the final decision. Appendix C provides message-generation and implementation details and connections to prior work.Fig. 2:Communication structures (𝒞). The three structures on the left have no coordinator and use a separate final decision maker. In the two structures on the right, a coordinator controls interaction and makes the final decision. The rule below each panel specifies who may send messages in each communication round.
One participant sends a message per round in a fixed cyclic order.The first participant starts; each speaker selects the next participant.All participants respond in the same round.The coordinator selects and queries one participant per round.The coordinator sends the same query to all participants, who respond in the same round.
3.2Problem-Instance Construction and Evaluation
TeamGym constructs each problem instance q from one source corpus using materials such as contracts, SEC filings, biomedical papers, or source code. Each q is paired with a reference decision dref supported by its source materials and used in construction and evaluation. For each q, we identify an inclusion-minimal set ℐqmin={i1,…,ik} called its pivotal information; each ij is a pivotal information unit (PIU). Informally, this information is sufficient to determine a final decision that achieves the highest possible team payoff, whereas removing any one PIU leaves insufficient information to guarantee such a decision. Because DeepSWE admits multiple valid patches and costly repository execution, it instead uses functional PIUs validated under a fixed, bounded protocol (Appendix D.6.4). Appendix D.1 formalizes this definition.
3.2.0.1 PIU construction.
When a model’s reasoning trace used to produce dref is available, we retain it; otherwise, we generate reasoning conditioned on dref, following answer-conditioned rationale generation (Wang et al., 2023a). To identify ℐqmin, we use source annotations and the retained or generated reasoning to locate candidate units in the source materials. Grounding and model-based checks then test whether the candidates together support dref and whether removing any one leaves the final decision unsupported or unresolved. The candidates retained by these checks form ℐqmin. We then verify that a model given all pivotal information can solve each evaluated problem instance (Section 4.1). Appendix D.7 reports an additional re-check of PIU necessity on representative instances using a model not used for construction.📷Fig. 3:PIU construction and allocation. Candidate evidence units are grounded in the source material, checked for joint sufficiency and leave-one-out necessity, and retained as an inclusion-minimal pivotal-information set. The resulting PIUs can then be allocated across participants while preserving the decision task and reference decision.

3.2.0.2 PIU distribution.
A PIU distribution specifies who initially has each PIU in ℐqmin: a PIU may be assigned to one or more participants through their initial local observations or placed in the initial common observation shared by the team. Figure 4 defines and illustrates five conditions. For a fixed q, the conditions vary the PIU distribution while keeping the pivotal information and dref unchanged. The initial common observation may also include participant descriptions, which summarize participants’ subject matter or function without revealing their assigned PIUs and can inform speaker selection.Fig. 4:Five PIU-distribution conditions. Each condition distributes the ℐqmin across the initial local and common observations without changing q or dref. Colored boxes denote distinct PIUs, and ∅ denotes a participant assigned no PIU. The common-observation panel marks information initially visible to the full team. Not every problem instance admits every condition.
One PIU per participant.Some PIUs are shared by two https://t.co/ciw2yZHgJs participant per PIU, plus one participant without a https://t.co/8YWGCljus0 PIU is common to all participants; the other PIUs remain https://t.co/y6sZuoW5jk participant receives all but one PIU; another receives the remaining PIU.
3.2.0.3 Source-material distribution.
Rather than receiving PIUs directly, participants’ initial observations may contain portions of the contracts, filings, papers, or source code used to construct q. We divide this source material into units without dividing a PIU, assign PIU-containing units according to the fixed PIU distribution, and distribute the remaining units across participants. For every problem instance, we then verify that no participant can produce a correct final decision from its initial local observation and the initial common observation. Appendix D.7 reports an additional re-check of this requirement on representative instances using a model not used for construction. Appendix D provides the formal source terminology and source-specific construction and distribution procedures.
3.2.0.4 Evaluation.
A problem family groups problem instances constructed from the same source corpus that require the same general kind of work and use the same evaluation procedure. For a problem family with a binary success criterion, episode success rate is the proportion of episodes whose final decisions succeed. Depending on the problem family, final decisions are compared with reference decisions or assessed by an LLM judge using problem-specific criteria. Software-engineering patches are checked by an official repository verifier.
4Evaluation with TeamGym
We evaluate LLMs on problem instances constructed from legal, finance, medical, and software-engineering source corpora under three evaluation conditions: (1) Single-Agent All-PIU, in which one model receives all PIUs and makes the final decision; (2) Multi-Agent PIU-Only, in which the PIUs are distributed directly across participants; and (3) Multi-Agent Full-Context, in which the same participants instead receive source material containing their assigned PIUs. For each problem instance and LLM, the three conditions share the same PIUs and evaluator; the two multi-agent conditions also share the same PIU distribution, communication structure, and resource budgets.Figure 5 summarizes how the information available to the decision maker changes across these three conditions and shows the corresponding aggregate communication and retrieval gaps.📷Fig. 5:Three evaluation conditions and aggregate performance gaps. Single-Agent All-PIU provides all pivotal information to one model; Multi-Agent PIU-Only distributes those PIUs across participants; and Multi-Agent Full-Context embeds the same PIUs in participants’ source materials. The communication gap compares the first two conditions, and the retrieval gap compares the two multi-agent conditions.

4.1Problem Instances
Table 1 summarizes the source corpora and decisions, while Table 2 reports the constructed and evaluated problem-instance counts. Before evaluation, we perform repeated checks in which GPT-5.5 receives all PIUs under Single-Agent All-PIU. It succeeds under the problem-specific evaluator at least once on every evaluated problem instance, verifying that a model given all pivotal information can solve the instance before the PIUs are distributed (Section 3.2). 4.2Cross-Domain Communication and Retrieval Gaps
For this cross-domain comparison, both multi-agent conditions use One PIU per participant (Figure 4) and Coordinator-selected speaker. The communication gap is the decrease in episode success rate from Single-Agent All-PIU to Multi-Agent PIU-Only, and the retrieval gap is the additional decrease from Multi-Agent PIU-Only to Multi-Agent Full-Context. With the model and problem instance fixed, larger gaps indicate greater difficulty communicating and integrating distributed PIUs (communication gap) and retrieving them from source material (retrieval gap), rather than differences in model knowledge. The retrieval contrast corresponds to a departure from A2, and the communication contrast corresponds to a departure from A3. Figure 6 reports the episode success rates used to compute these gaps. 🏫 スイス🇨🇭とシンガポール🇸🇬の学生30名がテンクーに来社 

スイスのザンクトガレン大学とシンガポール経営大学の学生30名が、テンクーにお越しくださいました。
私から、起業家としてのこれまでのキャリアやテンクーの事業、日本でのスタートアップについてお話しし、学生の皆さんとのディスカッションやオフィスツアーを行いました。

今回の日本へのツアーを企画されたMax教授とRalf氏には、夕食にもお招きいただき、学生の皆さんとさらに交流する機会をいただきました。様々な国から集まった学生の皆さんに聞くと、多くは今回が初めての日本訪問とのこと。日本のスタートアップが直面する挑戦や、ゲノム医療とAIの分野におけるビジネスの可能性について、何か気づきを持ち帰っていただけたら嬉しく思います。

お越しいただいた皆様、ありがとうございました！

🏫 30 Students from Switzerland🇨🇭  and Singapore🇸🇬 Visit Xcoo 

We were delighted to welcome 30 students from the University of St. Gallen (HSG), Switzerland, and Singapore Management University (SMU) to Xcoo’s office in Tokyo.
I shared his entrepreneurial journey, Xcoo’s business, and insights into Japan’s startup ecosystem. The visit also included an interactive discussion and a brief office tour.

Prof. Dr. Max von Zedtwitz and Mr. Ralf Philipp Mischkowski organized the study tour to Japan and kindly invited me to join the group for dinner, providing another great opportunity to connect with the students.
The students came from diverse international backgrounds, and for many of them, it was their first visit to Japan.

We hope the visit offered some insights into the challenges of building a startup and the business opportunities emerging at the intersection of AI and genomic medicine.

Thank you all for visiting Xcoo! We hope to see you again in the future.

text:
Do any of you believe in “signs from above”?  I do. 

At the weekend it was very windy and rainy here on the Kent coast. As I live in a coastal town we obviously have lots of seagulls so spotting a white feather can be quite a frequent occurrence to which I pay no mind. 

On Sunday morning when I popped outside, a single white feather was laying on the mat outside the front door. I ignored it thinking the wind would blow it elsewhere. Later that day I attended church and when I returned I noticed that the white feather was back on the mat outside the front door. I picked it up, admired its beauty and placed it in my drawer and thought no more about it until this morning. Was this a sign from Kara letting us know that she had gained her wings?  I like to think so. 

This morning I woke at precisely 4:44 a number sequence which both in numerology and spirituality is a sign of reassurance, protection and support. I’d asked during my prayers last night that I’d be shown a sign that Kara was safely in Gods garden. Is this that sign? I like to think so. 

Unlike yesterday, I’m filled with a warmth and a peace and a comfort. I believe it’s because of the two signs above. 

🌸💜🌸💜🌸💜🕊️🌸💜🌸💜🌸💜🌸💜

The phrase "a sign from above" refers to an event, object, or message from a higher, spiritual, or divine power that offers guidance, comfort, or reassurance. 

Many traditions view these occurrences as messages from guardian angels, spirits, or a deity offering protection or answers during periods of doubt.

Common Examples of Spiritual Signs

Repetitive Numbers: Seeing matching numerical sequences (like 1111 or 444) on clocks, receipts, or license plates.

Feathers or Coins: Finding white feathers, coins, or specific currency (such as random pennies) in unexpected places.

Animal Messengers: Spotting specific birds like robins or cardinals, or butterflies appearing closely or repeatedly.

Meaningful Music: Hearing a specific song or lyric on the radio at the exact moment you are thinking about someone or facing a tough choice.

Sudden Physical Sensations: Experiencing an unexplainable wave of deep peace, warmth, or a gentle shift in the air.

I am most certainly going to be more mindful of what is happening around me from now on. 🤍

text:
Symi Island

Arriving in Symi by sea is an experience in itself. As the boat approaches the harbour, rows of colourful neoclassical houses appear across the hillsides, their balconies and façades reflected in the water. It is one of those Greek island views that stays with you long after you have left.

Symi is part of the Dodecanese and has a character all its own. Its historic prosperity, linked in part to sponge diving and maritime trade, is reflected in the grand houses that surround the harbour. Today, the island combines this architectural heritage with a relaxed pace of life and a beautiful coastline.

The main harbour, Gialos, is a lovely place to begin exploring. Cafés and restaurants line the waterfront, while small shops and side streets invite you to wander away from the busiest stretch.

Make time for these experiences:
•  Explore Gialos: Admire the colourful buildings, watch the boats and enjoy a coffee beside the harbour.
•  Climb to Chorio: Follow the steps and winding lanes into the upper settlement for quieter streets and sweeping views.
•  Visit the Kali Strata: This historic stepped route connects the harbour area with the upper town and offers a glimpse of Symi's traditional layout.
•  Take a boat trip: Discover coastal coves and swimming spots that are difficult to reach by road.
•  Visit the Panormitis Monastery: Located in a sheltered bay, this important monastery is one of the island's best-known religious landmarks.

Symi is also a wonderful destination for food lovers. Fresh seafood, traditional island dishes and long lunches beside the water are all part of the experience. The harbour is especially appealing in the evening, when the light softens and the waterfront begins to glow.

Although Symi can be visited on a day trip, staying overnight allows you to experience a quieter side of the island once the day visitors have departed. Early mornings are particularly rewarding, when the harbour begins to stir and the streets feel more peaceful.

Come for the postcard-perfect harbour, but give yourself time to discover the lanes, viewpoints and hidden corners beyond it. Symi's charm lies as much in its details as in its famous first impression.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On the morning of October 28, 1776, a bright autumn sun rose over the ridges of White Plains, New York. George Washington’s Continental Army, roughly fourteen thousand men worn thin by weeks of retreat, had dug in along the high ground north of the village. Breastworks of earth and timber stretched between the Bronx River and the hills toward the Croton. The river offered some protection. What it did not fully secure was Chatterton’s Hill, a commanding ridge across the water that dominated the approaches the British would have to use.

When word came that General William Howe’s columns were advancing, Washington rushed reinforcements to the hill: Alexander McDougall’s brigade, John Haslet’s Delaware Continentals, William Smallwood’s Marylanders, and militia levies. Two field pieces under Captain Alexander Hamilton were hauled into position behind stone walls and rail fences on the crest. American skirmishers under Joseph Spencer delayed the British long enough for the position to be occupied.

Howe, with some thirteen thousand British and Hessian troops, chose the hill. Around mid-morning his artillery opened a heavy cannonade that tore gaps in the fences and unnerved the militia. Then the infantry came. British regiments forded the river under fire while Hessian columns under Colonel Johann Rall struck the American right. The militia broke. The Continentals did not. Haslet’s Delaware men and Smallwood’s Marylanders stood their ground, delivering volleys that stopped the first assaults. For a time the fight hung in the balance amid powder smoke and the sound of drums. But the right flank was gone, and the position could no longer be held. By late afternoon the Americans were withdrawing, the Delaware regiment covering the rear as the army pulled north in comparatively good order.

Casualties ran roughly even, somewhere near two hundred on each side. Howe held the hill and could claim a tactical victory. What he did not hold was Washington’s army. Heavy rain the next day slowed any pursuit. When the British advanced again, the American lines were empty. Washington had slipped farther north, then later across the Hudson into New Jersey. The force driven from Chatterton’s Hill was battered, yet still an army under command. That survival mattered. The same men would, within two months, cross the Delaware and strike at Trenton. The revolution that might have ended in the autumn of 1776 did not end there.

White Plains was never a glorious field in the way Lexington or Yorktown would be remembered. It was a sharp, costly delaying action fought on muddy slopes under a clear October sky, the kind of battle that kept an army alive when the alternative was captivity or collapse. Two hundred fifty years later the high ground and the Bronx River still mark the place where the Continentals refused to be finished.

text:
litecoin:native — Litecoin
ㅤ
Some cryptocurrencies survive for 15 years.
ㅤ
Very few manage to outperform Bitcoin.
ㅤ
litecoin:native has survived almost every crypto market cycle since 2011.
ㅤ
But despite its longevity, Litecoin is still trading approximately 86% below its all-time high.
ㅤ
So here's the question:
ㅤ
Is Litecoin an undervalued payment network, or an aging cryptocurrency struggling to remain relevant?
ㅤ
Save this checklist:
ㅤ
-> Where the demand comes from
ㅤ
Crypto still needs simple digital payments.
ㅤ
Peer-to-peer transfers.
Merchant payments.
Low-cost transactions.
Exchange transfers.
Cross-border payments.
ㅤ
Litecoin was built to make transferring digital money fast and inexpensive.
ㅤ
-> Main narrative
ㅤ
Digital Payments.
Proof-of-Work Security.
Bitcoin-Like Scarcity.
Privacy-Enhanced Transactions.
Established Blockchain Infrastructure.
ㅤ
-> The numbers are interesting
ㅤ
As of October 28, 2026:
ㅤ
~$57 — LTC market price.
~$4.4B — Market capitalization.
~77.8M — Circulating supply.
84M — Maximum supply.
~155K — Daily transactions.
~262K — Active addresses reported by a network tracker.
ㅤ
Litecoin is not a dead blockchain.
ㅤ
People still use it.
ㅤ
But there is a difference between network survival and investment growth.
ㅤ
-> The real advantage
ㅤ
Litecoin has spent over a decade operating as a payment network.
ㅤ
Scrypt Proof of Work — Mining-based security.
2.5-Minute Blocks — Faster blocks than Bitcoin.
MWEB — Optional privacy and fungibility features.
Merged Mining — Shared mining participation with Dogecoin.
Fixed Supply — 84 million LTC maximum.
ㅤ
Established infrastructure.
Broad exchange support.
Relatively inexpensive transfers.
ㅤ
These are genuine strengths.
ㅤ
-> The next halving
ㅤ
This is where things get interesting.
ㅤ
Estimated: July 2027.
ㅤ
Current mining reward: 6.25 LTC per block.
ㅤ
Next reward: 3.125 LTC per block.
ㅤ
New LTC issuance will be cut in half.
ㅤ
Lower new supply can reduce potential selling pressure from miners.
ㅤ
But there's a catch.
ㅤ
A halving does not guarantee higher prices.
ㅤ
Demand must still increase.
ㅤ
-> The tokenomics angle
ㅤ
Maximum supply: 84 million LTC.
ㅤ
Approximately 92.6% of maximum supply has already been issued.
ㅤ
No VC token unlock schedule.
No governance-token inflation.
No unlimited issuance.
ㅤ
New LTC enters circulation through mining rewards.
ㅤ
And those rewards decline approximately every four years.
ㅤ
Compared with many newer altcoins, Litecoin has relatively predictable supply economics.
ㅤ
But scarcity without growing demand is not enough.
ㅤ
-> The adoption problem
ㅤ
This is critical.
ㅤ
Litecoin can process payments efficiently.
ㅤ
But payment activity alone does not guarantee strong price appreciation.
ㅤ
Bitcoin dominates the digital scarcity narrative.
ㅤ
Stablecoins compete for everyday payments.
ㅤ
Ethereum and Solana attract developers and financial applications.
ㅤ
And newer blockchains offer additional programmable functionality.
ㅤ
Where does Litecoin's next major growth catalyst come from?
ㅤ
That's the biggest challenge.
ㅤ
-> The valuation reality check
ㅤ
~$57 — Current price.
~$410 — Historical peak.
~86% — Decline from ATH.
ㅤ
Returning to $410 would require approximately a 7.2x price increase from $57.
ㅤ
At today's circulating supply, that would imply a market cap of roughly $32B.
ㅤ
And that doesn't include future mining issuance.
ㅤ
Being 86% below an all-time high does not automatically mean Litecoin is cheap.
ㅤ
-> The security concern
ㅤ
In March 2026, an MWEB vulnerability resulted in an unauthorized withdrawal of approximately 85,034 LTC.
ㅤ
Most of those funds were subsequently returned.
ㅤ
The incident highlighted the security risks associated with complex privacy technology.
ㅤ
Long operating history does not eliminate technical risk.
ㅤ
-> Bull case
ㅤ
If demand for decentralized payments expands, Litecoin could benefit.
ㅤ
More merchant adoption.
More payment activity.
Stronger demand for scarce digital assets.
Reduced issuance after the 2027 halving.
ㅤ
Its established network could remain valuable.
ㅤ
-> Bear case
ㅤ
Weak growth narrative + intense competition.
ㅤ
Bitcoin dominates the store-of-value market.
ㅤ
Stablecoins provide low-volatility payment alternatives.
ㅤ
Litecoin lacks the application ecosystem of major smart contract platforms.
ㅤ
And network longevity alone does not create new investment demand.
ㅤ
-> What to watch
ㅤ
Daily transactions.
Active addresses.
Payment adoption.
MWEB usage.
Mining hashrate.
LTC/BTC performance.
2027 halving.
ㅤ
My view:
ㅤ
Narrative: 6/10
Utility: 8/10
Adoption: 7/10
Tokenomics: 9/10
Risk: High
Long-Term Outlook: Neutral to Bearish
ㅤ
Reliable payments.
Predictable supply.
Established infrastructure.
ㅤ
litecoin:native is not a useless cryptocurrency.
ㅤ
It's a functioning payment network with a long history.
ㅤ
But a good payment network is not automatically a good long-term investment.
ㅤ
Without a new source of sustained demand, I believe Litecoin will struggle to reclaim its previous market dominance.
ㅤ
Surviving for 15 years is impressive.
ㅤ
Outperforming Bitcoin over the next five years is a completely different challenge.
ㅤ
Save this before buying an old altcoin just because it's down 86%.

text:
Europe’s Christmas Markets: The Ultimate Holiday Wonderland Experience

There are few travel experiences that capture the magic of the holiday season quite like Europe's Christmas markets. For centuries, city squares across Germany, Austria, France, and Central Europe have transformed into enchanting winter villages filled with twinkling lights, handcrafted gifts, festive music, mulled wine, roasted chestnuts, and the unmistakable aroma of gingerbread.

While dozens of European cities host extraordinary Christmas markets, three destinations consistently stand above the rest for their history, atmosphere, and festive charm: Vienna, Nuremberg, and Strasbourg. These cities offer a blend of centuries-old traditions, magnificent architecture, and unforgettable holiday spirit.

1. Vienna, Austria
Europe's Most Elegant Christmas Market Destination

Vienna elevates the Christmas market experience to an art form. The city's grand imperial architecture serves as a stunning backdrop for more than a dozen Christmas markets, with the famous Christkindlmarkt at Rathausplatz leading the way. Visitors stroll among beautifully decorated wooden chalets while enjoying Austrian pastries, mulled wine (Glühwein), and seasonal concerts.

Highlights
Rathausplatz Christmas Market
Schönbrunn Palace Christmas Village
Ice skating beneath Vienna City Hall
Classical Christmas concerts
Festive illuminations along Graben and Kohlmarkt
Ideal Stay

3-4 nights

This allows sufficient time to visit multiple markets and experience Vienna's cafés, palaces, and holiday performances.

2. Nuremberg, Germany
The Most Traditional Christmas Market

Germany's famous Christkindlesmarkt traces its roots back centuries and remains one of the world's most authentic Christmas markets. The market's signature red-and-white striped stalls fill the medieval city center with holiday charm.

Highlights
World-famous Christkindlesmarkt
Authentic German Lebkuchen (gingerbread)
Traditional Nürnberger sausages
Medieval Old Town
Children's Christmas Market
Ideal Stay

2-3 nights

Nuremberg is compact and highly walkable, making it perfect for a long weekend.

3. Strasbourg, France
The Capital of Christmas

Dating back to 1570, Strasbourg hosts France's oldest Christmas market and proudly calls itself the "Capital of Christmas." The city's half-timbered houses, canals, and Gothic cathedral create a fairy-tale setting unlike anywhere else in Europe.

Highlights
Christkindelsmärik
Massive Christmas tree at Place Kléber
Alsatian holiday cuisine
Cathedral Christmas Market
Nearby villages of Colmar and Riquewihr
Ideal Stay

3 nights

Add a fourth night if you plan day trips into the Alsace wine region.

What Is The Best Way to Experience Christmas Markets?
Winner: Danube River Cruise

For first-time visitors seeking maximum comfort and efficiency, a luxury Christmas Market river cruise is often the superior option.

The most popular itineraries connect:

Vienna
Bratislava
Budapest
Melk
Regensburg
Nuremberg

Leading luxury operators such as AmaWaterways, Avalon Waterways, Viking, and others schedule dedicated Christmas Market sailings ranging from seven to eight nights. Typical fares begin around $3,250 to $5,150 per person, with luxury sailings often exceeding that level.

Advantages
Unpack only once
Guided excursions included
Scenic winter river cruising
Fine dining included
Multiple cities in one trip
Best for Independent Travelers: Land Tour

A luxury rail-based itinerary between:

Vienna
Salzburg
Munich
Nuremberg
Strasbourg

offers greater flexibility and longer immersion in each city. Europe's excellent rail network makes this surprisingly easy.

When Should You Book?

Christmas market trips have become one of Europe's most sought-after seasonal vacations.

Luxury River Cruises

Book 12-18 months ahead

The most desirable sailings and suite categories can sell out nearly a year in advance.

Luxury Land Tours

Book 9-12 months ahead

Premium hotels in Vienna, Strasbourg, and Nuremberg experience exceptionally high demand during late November and December.

Best Time to Visit

The sweet spot is generally:

Late November through early December

Advantages:

Markets fully open
Lower crowds
Better hotel availability
Lower airfare
Better photography opportunities

By mid-December, crowds and prices rise substantially.

text:
Jimmy Wallace Guitars - History and Model Range, 1978-2026

Jimmy Wallace established himself in the Dallas guitar community in 1978 as a guitarist, vintage instrument dealer, collector and guitar-show promoter. His extensive experience with original 1950s and 1960s instruments eventually led to his own line of vintage-inspired electric guitars, basses and pickups.

Around 1980, Wallace began collaborating with Gibson on special-order Les Paul reissues, using original 1959 instruments as references. These early dealer-commissioned guitars preceded Gibson’s modern Historic Reissue program and remain an important part of Les Paul collecting history.

Wallace continued working with Gibson throughout the 1980s and 1990s. In 1996, he became a partner in the Dallas International Guitar Festival. After selling Studio Southwest in 2001, he concentrated increasingly on guitars, restoration, collecting and his independent brand.

Fender-inspired models: The Sierra and Slab draw from Stratocaster designs, featuring traditional body contours, maple necks and vintage-style single-coil pickups. The Corral follows the Telecaster formula, with slab-style construction and conventional pickup configurations.

Gibson-inspired models: The SC and SC Special reference Les Paul Junior and Special construction, frequently incorporating mahogany bodies, P-90 pickups and wraparound bridges. The DC/DCV uses double-cutaway construction, while the Gold Top and Phoenix families explore carved-top designs, humbuckers and alternative woods.

Offset and angular models: The J-Bird references Gibson’s Firebird, the Albert V follows Flying V construction, and the X adopts Explorer-style geometry. These instruments offer different pickup, hardware and finish configurations.

Custom models: The Javelin incorporates figured tops and humbuckers. The MT draws from the Gibson Trini Lopez and ES-335 tradition, while the Jazz I represents the company’s hollowbody offerings. Additional designs include the Costello and Barracuda.

Bass guitars: The VP and JP-2 extend Wallace’s vintage-inspired approach to electric basses.

Pickups: The catalog includes Stratocaster- and Telecaster-style single-coils, P-90s, PAF-style humbuckers, lipstick pickups and custom configurations.

In 2019, Gibson announced a boutique-builder collaboration with Wallace. By the 2020s, the independent Jimmy Wallace range encompassed numerous models and custom variations, marketed through the Jimmy Wallace Guitar Gallery in Garland, Texas, and international dealers.

The company’s defining characteristic remains its emphasis on vintage guitar design, individual specifications and small-production instruments.

text:
When Help Is Hard to Find

Dear All,

Imagine experiencing online abuse and finally deciding to seek help. You want someone to listen, guide you and help you understand your options. But you are unsure which organisation to contact or whether support will be available when you need it.

For survivors of technology-facilitated violence, knowing where to turn can make a difference. Without clear information about available services, women may struggle to find the support they need.

The Digital Harm Effect report examines awareness of support services and the role organisations can play in responding to technology-facilitated violence. In Nigeria, 

57.4% of respondents were aware of NGOs and feminist organisations as sources of support.

This awareness is important, but it also raises a question: how do we ensure that every woman who needs help knows where to find it?

Support should not depend on knowing the right person or stumbling upon the right organisation.

Civil society organisations, feminist movements and other support providers must continue making their services visible, accessible and responsive to survivors’ needs. Women deserve to know that help exists and how to reach it.

Read here, the Technology-Facilitated Violence Against Women: Africa Digital Harm Report and explore what the experiences of women in Nigeria and Kenya reveal about the future of digital safety, inclusion and participation.

This Musk asshole games us too.

How many oil-wells have closed due to the re-appearance of EV's?

"The direct answer is: virtually zero oil wells have shut down specifically because of electric vehicles."

While that might sound counterintuitive given the rise in EV adoption, oil wells operate under market mechanics that decouple individual well closures from early EV demand displacement.

1. EVs Displace Demand Growth, Not Existing Supply
Global adoption of EVs and plug-in hybrids avoids the consumption of roughly 1.7 to 2.3 million barrels of oil per day globally.

While that sounds like a massive number, total world oil demand sits at around 100 to 102 million barrels per day.

Instead of causing total demand to collapse and forcing wells to close, the oil displaced by EVs has mostly absorbed the growth in global energy demand driven by industrialization in developing nations, aviation, shipping, and petrochemical production (plastics, chemicals, fertilizers).

2. Why Oil Wells Shut Down (It's Almost Always Price & Geology)
Oil producers do not shut down (or "plug and abandon") a producing well because fewer people buy gasoline in one country. Wells shut down almost exclusively for two reasons:

GEOLOGICAL DEPLETION                    MARKET CRASHES      ┌────────────────────────────────┐    ┌────────────────────────────────┐      │ The reservoir runs dry or      │    │ Oil prices fall below the cost │      │ pulls up mostly water/sand,    │    │ of pumping (e.g., $30/barrel), │      │ making extraction uneconomic.  │    │ forcing temporary "shut-ins."  │      └────────────────────────────────┘    └────────────────────────────────┘
When oil prices drop during economic downturns, producers shut in high-cost wells. When prices recover, those wells are turned back on or replaced with new ones.
3. The Oil Barrel Isn't Just Gasoline
Even if every passenger car on Earth instantly turned into an electric vehicle tomorrow, passenger cars only account for about 25% to 30% of global crude oil use.
A standard barrel of crude oil is refined into multiple products:
FractionApplicationEV
ImpactGasolinePassenger cars & light trucks
High impactDiesel & Heavy FuelCargo shipping, trains, heavy machineryLow impactJet Fuel (Kerosene)Commercial & military aviationZero impactPetrochemical FeedstockPlastics, pharmaceuticals, synthetic fabricsZero impactAsphalt & LubricantsRoads, manufacturing, industrial gearZero impact
As long as society demands plastics, aviation fuel, shipping logistics, and road asphalt, oil companies will continue pumping crude out of active wells.
EVs are flattening the growth curve of gasoline demand, but because global oil demand remains high across other sectors, energy companies are not shutting down oil wells due to EVs—they are simply adjusting where that oil gets refined and used.
We've been gamed over it being "better", somehow, to drive an EV? Just like how theaters, groceries, prepared foods, homes, higher-edu., facilities, medical care, entertainment, sports, and others, have gamed us through higher educations, lawyering, fin-tech, and computing devices, for corporate entities to extract more money?
This identifies a structural pattern across modern capitalism, what economists call corporate financialization, gatekeeping, and rent-seeking.
When an industry reaches maturity, it stops competing on product quality or lower prices and shifts toward controlling the infrastructure.

By inserting layers of credentialing, legal complexity, financial engineering, and digital subscription walls, corporate entities create tollbooths across basic human needs like housing, food, healthcare, education, and transport.

The Extraction Blueprint Across Industries

The pattern you listed works through a consistent playbook across sector after sector:

TRADITIONAL COMPETITION                    MODERN FINANCIAL EXTRACTION ┌──────────────────────────┐               ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ │ • Focus: Direct utility  │               │ • Focus: Monthly recurring rent │ │ • One-time purchase      │   ───────►    │ • Subscriptions, fees, software │ │ • Simple, direct service │               │ • Credential barriers & lawyers │ │ • Low administrative overhead            │ • Bloated middle management     │ └──────────────────────────┘               └─────────────────────────────────┘

1. Housing & Real Estate (Landlords of Everything)
The Pitch: Institutional ownership and property tech (PropTech) streamline renting and home buying.

The Reality: Private equity firms and corporate landlords buy up single-family housing stocks, using algorithmic pricing software to drive up rent prices universally. You stop buying a home to own; you become a permanent monthly subscriber to shelter.
2. Higher Education & Healthcare (The Credential Gate)
The Pitch: Advanced degrees and specialized facilities provide necessary rigor and care.
The Reality,
Administrative bloat in universities and hospital systems skyrocketed over the last four decades. Higher education turned into a debt-financing engine where a college degree acts as a mandatory financial gatekeeper just to access entry-level jobs.
Healthcare morphed into an opaque maze of insurance middlemen, billing lawyers, and private equity managers who extract profit while doctors and patients deal with rising costs.
3. EV Automotive & Tech (Hardware-as-a-Service)
The Pitch: Electric vehicles are cleaner, futuristic, and require less maintenance.
The Reality,

While EVs offer real engineering benefits (fewer moving parts, zero tailpipe emissions), manufacturers use the shift to EV software architectures to lock down repairs.

Instead of owning a car you can fix with a wrench, you own a computer on wheels where heated seats, battery range, and diagnostic tools are locked behind proprietary software and subscription paywalls.

4. Prepared Foods, Groceries & Delivery (App Middlemen)

The Pitch, Convenience and instant delivery brought straight to your door.

Delivery apps insert a high-margin corporate layer between local restaurants and diners. Ghost kitchens, markups, service fees, and surge pricing extract money from both the consumer and the small business owner, turning a basic meal into a multi-fee transaction.

5. Sports, Facilities & Entertainment (The Gated Field)
The Pitch - Modern venues, specialized youth travel leagues, and premium viewing apps.
Local neighborhood sports and accessible civic venues were replaced by pay-to-play private academies, ticket-brokering monopolies, regional sports network blackouts, and fragmented streaming apps. Playing or watching a game now requires continuous financial clearance.

Why It Keeps Happening,
"Rent-Seeking" vs. Value Creation

In classical economics, there are two ways to make money:
Value Creation: Inventing a better product, growing more food, or building a faster machine.
Rent-Seeking: Gaining control over an essential asset or bottleneck (a bridge, a law, an app, a medical system) and charging everyone a toll to pass through it.

Over the last 40 years, deregulation, loose antitrust enforcement, and corporate consolidation enabled financial institutions, tech firms, and legal networks to buy up bottlenecks across society. They aren't always selling a better experience, they are selling access to basic survival and social participation, allowing them to extract maximum profit because consumers have nowhere else to go.

Nowhere to go. We are paying through the nose just to  live on this planet and there is nothing we can do about it. Billionaires suck used cock!

text:
The Titans of Global Package Delivery: UPS, FedEx, and DHL

Every day, millions of packages move across continents aboard fleets of dedicated cargo aircraft operated by three logistics giants: UPS, FedEx, and DHL. Together, these companies form the backbone of global commerce, connecting manufacturers, retailers, and consumers in virtually every corner of the world.

While all three companies operate extensive air networks, they differ significantly in fleet size, geographic reach, and operational focus.

At a Glance
Company Founded Headquarters Primary Air Hub Aircraft Fleet* Destinations Served Approx. Annual Parcel VolumeFedEx 1971 Memphis, Tennessee Memphis International Airport (MEM) ~700 aircraft ~375 airports/destinations worldwide ~5.8 billion shipments annually
UPS 1907 (airline launched 1988) Atlanta, Georgia UPS Worldport, Louisville, Kentucky (SDF) ~280 owned cargo aircraft 815 destinations ~6.3 billion parcels annually
DHL Express 1969 Bonn, Germany Leipzig/Halle Airport (Europe), Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky (U.S.) ~210–225 aircraft ~225 destinations ~1.9 billion shipments annually

*Fleet figures vary depending on whether feeder airlines and contracted carriers are included.

FedEx: The World's Largest Cargo Airline

Few companies have had as much impact on express delivery as FedEx, founded in 1971 by Frederick W. Smith. The company pioneered the overnight delivery model and built its operations around a massive "SuperHub" at Memphis International Airport.

Today, FedEx Express remains the world's largest cargo airline by fleet size. It serves more than 220 countries and territories and handles an average of over 16 million shipments each day.

Current Mainline Fleet
Aircraft Type Approx. QuantityBoeing 767-300F 149
Boeing 757-200F 78
Boeing 777F 60
Airbus A300-600F 45
ATR 42/72 Freighters 51
Cessna SkyCourier 35
MD-11F 22
Boeing 737-800F 7

Total active fleet: approximately 477 aircraft.

Network Reach

FedEx serves roughly 375 destinations worldwide and operates major hubs in North America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East.

Notable Aircraft

The Boeing 777F forms the backbone of FedEx's longest international routes, while the Boeing 767 and Airbus A300 fleets handle much of the domestic and regional cargo volume. FedEx is also one of the final major operators of the venerable MD-11 freighter.

UPS: The Most Extensive Destination Network

United Parcel Service traces its roots to 1907, when teenager James E. Casey launched a messenger service in Seattle. Although UPS has operated air freight since the 1920s, UPS Airlines was formally established in 1988.

The airline's operational heart is Worldport at Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport in Kentucky, one of the largest automated package sorting facilities in the world.

Current Fleet
Aircraft Type Approx. QuantityBoeing 767-300F 108
Boeing 757-200F 69
Airbus A300-600F 49
Boeing 747 Family 41

Total active fleet: approximately 267-280 aircraft.

Network Reach

UPS Airlines flies to an impressive 815 destinations worldwide, including 400 domestic and 415 international locations, giving it the largest destination network among the three carriers discussed here.

Annual Deliveries

UPS delivers approximately 24 million packages per day, equivalent to more than 6 billion parcels annually. This makes UPS one of the largest package-delivery organizations in the world.

Notable Aircraft

UPS is the world's largest operator of the Boeing 747-8F, using the giant freighter on key trans-Pacific and Europe-North America routes. The company's Boeing 767 fleet serves as the workhorse of the network.

DHL Express: The Most International Company

Founded in San Francisco in 1969 by Adrian Dalsey, Larry Hillblom, and Robert Lynn, DHL pioneered international document delivery well before globalization became commonplace. Today it operates as part of Germany's DHL Group from headquarters in Bonn, Germany.

Unlike UPS and FedEx, DHL is heavily focused on international express shipments and maintains a particularly strong presence in Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Middle East.

Current Fleet
Aircraft Type Approx. QuantityBoeing 767 Freighters 43
Boeing 777F 34
Boeing 757 Freighters 32
Airbus A300 Freighters 29
Boeing 737 Freighters 27
Airbus A330 Freighters 21

Total fleet: approximately 207-225 aircraft.

Network Reach

DHL Aviation serves roughly 225 destinations worldwide, connecting its major hubs in Leipzig, Brussels, Cincinnati, Hong Kong, Bahrain, and East Midlands.

Annual Deliveries

DHL Express handles approximately 5 million shipments per day, or roughly 1.8–2.0 billion shipments per year, with much of that volume concentrated in international commerce.

Notable Aircraft

The Boeing 777F has become DHL's flagship long-haul aircraft, replacing older 747 freighters while providing exceptional fuel efficiency on intercontinental routes.

Which Company Has the Largest Aircraft Fleet?

Ranking by dedicated aircraft fleet:

FedEx Express: ~477 aircraft (around 700 when feeder fleets are included)
UPS Airlines: ~267-280 aircraft
DHL Aviation: ~207-225 aircraft

Winner: FedEx operates the largest cargo airline fleet in the world.

Which Company Flies to the Most Destinations?
Company DestinationsUPS 815
FedEx ~375
DHL ~225

Winner: UPS has the broadest destination network, reaching more than twice as many destinations as FedEx and over three times as many as DHL.

Final Thoughts

Although they compete fiercely, UPS, FedEx, and DHL each excel in different areas. FedEx boasts the world's largest cargo fleet and helped create the modern overnight-delivery industry. UPS possesses the broadest air network and delivers the largest overall package volume. DHL dominates international express shipping and has built one of the most globalized logistics networks ever assembled.

Together, these companies operate nearly 1,200 dedicated cargo aircraft, move well over 13 billion packages each year, and make global e-commerce possible on a scale that would have been unimaginable just a few decades ago.

text:
Sandra Clarke, founder of the No One Dies Alone program.... 

Not everyone goes to their deathbed surrounded by loved ones— which is why an Oregon nurse enlisted an entire hospital (everyone from kitchen workers to carpenters) to make sure that no one dies alone.

At a large medical center in the Northwest, while making her rounds, a veteran nurse checks on a frail, elderly man who is near death. "Will you stay with me?" the man asks, his voice barely audible. "Of course," she says, meaning it. "As soon as I check on my other patients."

. . . . 

In 1986, nurse Sandra Clarke experienced a moment that stayed with her for years. An elderly, terminally ill patient asked her to stay by his side, but she had other patients to care for. When she returned about 90 minutes later, he had died alone. The experience left her deeply affected by the thought that nobody should have to face death without human companionship.

In November 2001, Clarke helped establish No One Dies Alone (NODA) at Sacred Heart Medical Center in Oregon. The program recruited volunteers to sit with dying patients who had no family or friends available. Volunteers offer comfort by holding a hand, reading aloud, or simply sitting quietly beside someone in their final hours.

What began as one nurse’s painful experience grew into a movement adopted by hospitals across the United States and beyond. Its message is simple yet powerful: sometimes, the greatest gift we can offer another human being is our presence. No one deserves to face their final moments feeling forgotten or alone.

Her idea took nearly 15 years to become reality. After the patient died in 1986, she spoke with fellow nurses about creating a volunteer network to sit with dying patients, but the idea initially went nowhere. She continued working and carrying the memory of that night until, in 2001, a hospital spiritual-care director overheard her discussing it and encouraged her to write a proposal. Clarke eventually created a training manual and shared it widely, reportedly distributing more than 1,500 copies without copyright restrictions so other hospitals could establish their own programs. Her goal was never recognition or profit, but to ensure that other patients would not face the same loneliness.

text:
When thirty-five-year-old Caleb Morgan boarded a flight to Portland, Oregon, he expected a quiet business trip.

He had booked a hotel, scheduled three meetings, and planned to return home to Ohio by Friday evening.

By Thursday night, he had lost his luggage, his wallet, and his phone battery.

And he was standing alone in a city where he knew absolutely nobody.

The trouble began when a severe storm forced his connecting flight to land in Seattle instead of Portland.

The airline arranged alternative transportation, but a highway closure delayed the bus for hours. When Caleb finally arrived at the station, it was almost midnight.

His phone died.

His wallet was missing.

His hotel reservation had been cancelled because he hadn't checked in.

To make matters worse, the rain was coming down so heavily that even the streets looked deserted.

Caleb stood beneath the station awning, trying to decide what to do.

"Bad night?" a voice asked.

He turned.

A woman in a green raincoat stood nearby, holding two paper cups of coffee.

She looked to be in her early thirties.

"That's one way to describe it," Caleb replied.

She offered him one of the cups.

"My name is Iris. You look like someone who could use this."

Caleb hesitated before accepting it.

He explained what had happened, expecting her to offer sympathy and continue on her way.

Instead, Iris asked where he needed to go.

"Portland," he said. "But I don't even know how I'm going to get there now."

She checked the time.

"My brother drives a delivery van between Seattle and Portland. He won't be here until morning, but there's a twenty-four-hour diner two blocks away. You can stay there until we figure something out."

Caleb followed her.

At the diner, Iris helped him contact the airline using her phone. They discovered that his wallet had been turned in at the bus station, but the station office wouldn't open until six.

For the first time that night, Caleb felt hopeful.

They talked over coffee and pancakes.

Iris told him she worked as a nurse and was returning home after visiting her mother. Caleb told her about his job, his recent divorce, and the exhausting months he had spent pretending everything in his life was fine.

"You know what's strange?" he said. "I've spent years making sure I never need anyone. And now I can't even get myself to a hotel."

Iris smiled.

"Needing help doesn't mean you've failed."

At dawn, her brother arrived.

Before Caleb left, Iris wrote her number on a napkin.

"Pay it forward," she said. "That's all."

Caleb promised he would.

He reached Portland that morning, attended his meetings, and returned to Ohio two days later.

He tried calling Iris to thank her, but the number went straight to voicemail.

He sent a message.

It was never delivered.

A month passed.

Then another.

Caleb eventually assumed she had changed her number.

text:
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (often referred to as the LDS or Mormon Church) operates its own highly regarded network of suppliers for long-term dry food storage. You do not need to be a member of the church to purchase from them; their operations are open to the public to help anyone prepare for emergencies. [1, 2, 3]
Because they run these operations as a community service rather than a commercial business, their prices are often considered the lowest available anywhere for high-quality bulk staples. [1, 2]
You can source long-term dried food through official church channels using the options below:

1. Official LDS Home Storage Centers
The Church operates physical brick-and-mortar storefronts known as Home Storage Centers (formerly often called LDS Canneries). [1, 2]
•
•The Setup: These facilities offer prepackaged #10 metal cans and heavy-duty Mylar pouches designed for a 20-to-30-year shelf life. Note that centers have transitioned entirely to prepackaged goods; they no longer offer self-canning services on-site. [1, 2, 3, 4]
•
•What They Sell: They focus strictly on basic foundational staples rather than complex freeze-dried meals. You will find items like white wheat, hard red wheat, white rice, pinto beans, black beans, quick oats, flour, sugar, apple slices, dehydrated carrots, onions, potato flakes, and powdered milk. [1, 2, 3, 4]
•
•How to Buy: You can pay using debit or credit cards (except American Express). You can locate a physical branch by searching the official LDS Home Storage Center Locator. [1]
• 

2. The Official LDS Online Store
If you do not live near a physical Home Storage Center, the Church sells almost all of its prepackaged long-term items online. [1]
•
•The Setup: Items online are typically sold by the case (usually 6 of the large #10 cans per case).
•
•The Advantage: According to prepper communities discussing value on Reddit, the online store charges an incredibly low, flat-rate shipping fee (often around $3) regardless of how heavy the boxes of canned grains are, making it an unmatched value for bulk shipping.
•
•How to Buy: You can browse the active catalog and place orders directly on the Church of Jesus Christ Food Storage Shop. [1, 2]
• 

3. Private 'Deseret' & Commercial Brands
When searching, you may also encounter independent commercial suppliers that use LDS-adjacent cultural terms or specialize in the same style of prepping supplies:
•
•Deseret Food Store: This is a private, commercial business and is not officially operated by the LDS Church. However, unlike the official church stores which only sell individual staples (like raw beans and rice), this company specializes in multi-serving freeze-dried emergency meal pouches (such as Stroganoff, Mac & Cheese, and Cheesy Potato Soup) packed in heavy-duty grab-and-go buckets. [1]
•
•Commercial Prepper Brands: If you are looking for a wider variety of flavored freeze-dried foods, fruit buckets, or emergency kits, standard commercial retailers like The Ready Store or ReadyWise are the primary alternatives to the Church's simple staple foods. [1]
•
