text:
Paisley Park Announces Exclusive Cory Wong & the Wongnotes Session Premiere

Sender: Paisley Park (@PaisleyPark)
Date: October 28, 2021
Time: 17:19:42 GMT
Subject: Tune in tonight at 7PM CST to check out @corywong & the Wongnotes play an incredible blend of soul, funk and jazz.
Link:

On October 28, 2021, the official Paisley Park account shared a post promoting an exclusive livestream premiere of guitarist Cory Wong and his band, the Wongnotes, performing from Studio A at Prince’s legendary Chanhassen, Minnesota complex. The short message invited fans to tune in at 7PM CST for a blend of soul, funk, and jazz, accompanied by two images: a purple promotional graphic for “Cory Wong – The Paisley Park Session – Exclusive Premiere 10.28.21” and a close-up of a white Cloud guitar.

This event marked the video premiere of Wong’s live album The Paisley Park Session, recorded earlier that year in the same Studio A space that served as Prince’s creative sanctuary. The album dropped the following day (October 29) across streaming platforms, featuring tracks such as “Welcome 2 Minneapolis,” “Assassin,” “Meditation,” and a cover of Vulfpeck’s “Dean Town.” The full-length video was available for a limited time via Mandolin, allowing viewers to experience the session as captured on site.

Wong, a Grammy-nominated Minneapolis-area guitarist known for his rhythmic funk style and work with Vulfpeck, described the experience as a joyous return to a place near his hometown. The band included bassist Sonny T (a longtime Prince collaborator), the Hornheads horn section, and other musicians. Notably, Wong performed on a signature Cloud guitar—modeled after the iconic instrument Prince used throughout his career, originally built in the early 1980s by Minneapolis luthier Dave Rusan and later produced in limited quantities. The Cloud’s distinctive curved body and association with Purple Rain made its presence in the session especially resonant.

The post highlighted how Paisley Park continued to function as a working studio and cultural hub after Prince’s 2016 death, hosting new music that bridged contemporary funk with the facility’s history. The livestream offered fans a rare look inside the space while celebrating the intersection of Wong’s high-energy instrumental approach and the Purple One’s legacy. The album and session footage later circulated widely, with individual tracks accumulating hundreds of thousands of views and the project standing as a notable post-Prince recording at the site. https://t.co/bVAbCo9aTV

text:
Paxton flips Texas Children’s Hospital from transgender hub to detransition clinic | Joseph MacKinnon, Blaze Media

A hospital that was just a few years ago performing sex-rejection procedures on minors has been forced to help its victims for free.

Texas has successfully transformed one of the main operating bases of the "trans" regime into a refuge for the regime's victims.

Quick background

Despite chatter in 2022 about ending the practice, physicians at Texas Children's Hospital in Houston continued performing sex-rejection interventions on minors.

'A clinic cannot give me back what I lost, but it can help patients rebuild their lives.'

In 2023, following whistleblower revelations about the ongoing sex-rejection interventions at Texas Children's Hospital, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton launched an investigation into it.

A lengthy investigation by his office's Healthcare Program Enforcement Division then ensued, and Paxton secured a settlement with Texas Children's Hospital earlier this year.

The hospital was required, among other things, to:

- permanently cease "providing, directly or indirectly, any sex-rejecting procedures" and referring patients to third parties for such medical procedures;

- revoke the privileges of and fire physicians who were involved in the hospital's sex-rejection operations; and

- pay nearly $10 million in civil penalties to "resolve claims brought under the Texas Health Care Program Fraud Prevention Act and the federal False Claims Act for billing Texas Medicaid for unallowable and illegal 'gender-transition' interventions."

Per the terms of the settlement, Texas Children's Hospital was also required to establish a detransition clinic to "help patients reverse the damage caused by ideologically motivated physicians who harmed patients by performing dangerous medical interventions for the purpose of 'transitioning' them."

First in the nation

Paxton announced on Tuesday that Texas Children's has opened the detransition clinic.

Chloe Cole, a detransitioner who has raised awareness about the horrors of sex-rejection medical interventions, told Blaze News, "Texas Children’s accepting appointment requests for detransition care is significant because people living with the consequences of transition deserve to be taken seriously."

"A clinic cannot give me back what I lost, but it can help patients rebuild their lives," continued Cole. "The medical system has a responsibility to care for the people who trusted it, including when those patients regret what was done to them."

According to Texas Children's, the clinic offers a team of multi-disciplinary experts with specialties including endocrinology, surgery, primary care, fertility counseling, psychiatry, and speech pathology.

The hospital is obligated to provide all care at no cost to patients for the next five years. To fund services beyond the initial five-year window, the hospital must include the detransition clinic as a specific gift designation on its "Giving" webpage.

Paxton vowed that he will "ensure that this clinic provides the care and support that victims of the radical left’s gender ideology deserve."

"This is an important step toward caring for a group of patients who have long been overlooked," Dr. Kurt Miceli, chief medical officer at the medical advocacy group Do No Harm, said in a statement to Blaze News. "Detransitioners have suffered because of the lies sold to them by transgender activists. Their struggles were often dismissed or ignored by the medical establishment. Yet they deserve as much support and care as we can give."

Miceli added, "The Detransition Clinic at Texas Children’s is a step in the right direction. We hope to see more hospitals open similar clinics, without the Department of Justice having to step in."

Cole suggested that the establishment of a detransition clinic presents a great opportunity "for research into improving life after transition."

"There are serious unanswered questions about how best to care for detransitioners," Cole told Blaze News. "If Texas Children’s is going to serve these patients properly, it needs to confront those questions: Which treatments actually help? What can realistically be restored? How do patients’ physical and psychological needs change over time?"

The clinic should be judged on whether it materially helps victims and whether it advances that knowledge, said Cole.

Paxton, who faces off with a supporter of the sex-rejection regime in the race for a seat in the U.S. Senate next week, said on Tuesday, "We will protect our children and defeat the dangerous ideology that has inflicted irreversible harm on innocent kids."

Texas Children's did not immediately respond to Blaze News' request for comment.

Just a week away from Election Day, Democrat James Talarico still holds a slight edge over Paxton in the Texas U.S. Senate race, according to Blaze News' Poll Watch.

text:
I lived in California for years, and Kaiser was one of the FEW things I genuinely loved about living there. 😂

Their vertical integration is something the entire healthcare industry should copy.

Here’s a real example.

You visit your primary care doctor. He notices a suspicious mole.

“Want a dermatologist to look at that?”

He checks his computer.

“Great, she’ll be here in 10 minutes.”

And the dermatologist literally walks into the SAME ROOM.

No driving across town. No filling out another 15 pages of paperwork.

Primary care, specialists, blood work, X-rays, MRIs. All connected, often in the same facility.

ONE system. ONE medical record.

Brilliant.

Now compare that to my experience with other providers in Miami.

Drive 45 minutes to see a doctor.

Wait an hour.

Doctor spends 5 minutes with you.

Refers you to another specialist 50 minutes away.

New office. New check-in system. New paperwork.

Name. Address. Insurance. Medical history.

AGAIN.

It’s 2026, and we’re still filling out the same information on paper like it’s 1995. 🤦‍♂️

At this point, just send me a link and let AI fill it out.

And here’s another interesting comparison.

When I visit Poland, I often skip the public system and pay cash for private healthcare.

The experience has been incredible.

I remember getting imaging done for around $100, with an appointment available the next day.

Modern facility. Professional staff. Fast results.

I’ve also paid roughly $300 for a full-body MRI.

But here’s the experience that really changed my perspective.

My wife once needed a fairly complicated procedure under general anesthesia.

We consulted multiple doctors in the US.

They explained that the tissue involved was so attached to the surrounding structures that removing it would require removing the entire organ.

That was the treatment approach they recommended.

We decided to get another opinion in Poland. 🇵🇱

The Polish specialists offered a different approach.

They were able to remove the problematic tissue while PRESERVING THE ORGAN.

And the total cost?

Around $5,000.

Including 2–3 days at a private clinic.

Excellent doctors. Modern facilities. Great care.

And a fraction of what we expected to pay in the US.

But here’s something interesting I’ve noticed recently.

I think the US healthcare market is slowly becoming more open to cash-paying patients too.

I’ve been paying cash for medical services in the US for about a year now.

And honestly?

I’m surprised how affordable some services can be when you skip insurance entirely.

Sometimes the cash price is almost identical to what my copay would’ve been WITH insurance. 😂

And more and more doctors seem perfectly comfortable with cash-paying patients.

You tell them you don’t have insurance and want to pay directly?

No big deal.

They already have a self-pay price ready.

No insurance approvals. No claims. No guessing what the bill will look like weeks later.

I really like that.

Obviously, paying cash for routine care doesn’t replace protection against a major medical emergency.

But for everyday medical services, having transparent cash prices and the freedom to shop around is a huge improvement.

I’m not claiming every hospital in Poland is better than every hospital in America.

But these experiences taught me something.

The problem isn’t necessarily the doctors.

It’s the SYSTEM surrounding them.

Kaiser showed me how efficient healthcare can be when everything works together.

Poland showed me how affordable private healthcare can be when you pay directly.

And now I’m seeing more of that cash-pay flexibility here in the US.

Meanwhile, much of the American healthcare system somehow manages to be expensive, fragmented, AND inefficient.

How did we make something so simple so complicated? 😂

🇺🇸 FL | Miami 2027: The New Geography of Power

Miami has always reinvented itself. Once a gateway to Latin America, it is now emerging as a crossroads where American diplomacy, global capital and transnational political networks intersect, bringing seemingly unrelated actors and agendas into the same orbit. Its latest transformation may be less about geography than about influence.

The pattern is becoming increasingly visible. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have been involved in high-level discussions with Russian, Ukrainian, European and Middle Eastern officials, with South Florida serving as a venue for negotiations over Ukraine and Gaza. This approach relies heavily on personal relationships and trusted intermediaries, with political negotiations often linked to economic incentives.

The geography helps explain Miami’s appeal. The city combines Latin American diaspora communities, conservative political networks, deep financial infrastructure and easy access to Washington. International negotiations and domestic political movements can operate side by side — and sometimes intersect.

The Brazilian dimension adds another layer. Following his defeat to Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro arrived in the United States after visas were confirmed for him and his family. In South Florida, the Bolsonaro family can draw on an established Brazilian diaspora, political allies and business networks cultivated over the years by their father, Jair Bolsonaro. These connections offer a platform for continued political visibility, transnational mobilisation and engagement with the US administration.

Yet Miami’s significance extends well beyond Latin America. Renewed Arab interest in American diplomacy, investment and regional security adds another dimension, as Gulf capital and Middle Eastern diplomatic initiatives intersect with broader discussions about reconstruction, energy infrastructure and regional stability. These parallel networks may converge in Miami without forming part of a single geopolitical project. The question is whether proximity and personal connections will translate into lasting cooperation.

That distinction matters. Personal diplomacy can open doors, but it can also blur the boundaries between public authority, private interests and political influence. Lasting agreements still require institutions, enforceable commitments and accountability.

Three tests will determine whether Miami’s influence endures: whether talks translate into lasting agreements, whether access to power survives the ebb and flow of personal relationships and political favour, and whether democratic oversight can keep pace with increasingly informal diplomacy.

Miami’s power lies in its connections, not its formal authority. A switchboard is not a capital: it routes power without owning it. And in a city defined by reinvention, the next chapter will depend on whether those connections can turn access into lasting influence.

text:
Doeren says goodbye to NC State, urges resources to match football expectations

Raleigh, NC – Dave Doeren offered thanks, accepted responsibility for a disappointing season and delivered a pointed message about the financial demands of modern college football Tuesday, closing his tenure at NC State with an appeal for the university to give its next coach the resources needed to meet expectations.

Speaking publicly after his dismissal, Doeren described a program that had become his family’s home and a profession increasingly shaped by the cost of acquiring and retaining players. He defended the broader accomplishments of his tenure while acknowledging that the championship he wanted to bring to Raleigh remained beyond reach.
photo by Gene Galin

“For this program to become what is wanted and expected, the resources need to match the expectations,” he said.

NC State announced Doeren’s dismissal Oct. 24 and appointed running backs coach and special teams coordinator Todd Goebbel as interim head coach for the remainder of the season. Athletics director Boo Corrigan said a national search for a successor would begin immediately.

Doeren’s farewell, delivered without a question-and-answer session, was both a personal accounting and an argument about the conditions facing his successor. He thanked players, staff members, university leaders, high school coaches and fans, then asked supporters to stand behind a team with five regular-season games remaining.

He also made clear that losing his job had not ended his attachment to NC State.

“I leave here with no grudges,” he said. “I completely love this place.”

NC State announced Doeren’s dismissal Oct. 24 and appointed running backs coach and special teams coordinator Todd Goebbel as interim head coach for the remainder of the season. Athletics director Boo Corrigan said a national search for a successor would begin immediately.

Doeren’s farewell, delivered without a question-and-answer session, was both a personal accounting and an argument about the conditions facing his successor. He thanked players, staff members, university leaders, high school coaches and fans, then asked supporters to stand behind a team with five regular-season games remaining.

He also made clear that losing his job had not ended his attachment to NC State.

“I leave here with no grudges,” he said. “I completely love this place.”

text:
Teodoro lauds US for 'sustained engagement' with ASEAN

MANILA – Department of National Defense (DND) Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Wednesday cited the United States’ "sustained engagement" with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which he credits for peace and stability in the region.

"We value the United States' sustained engagement with the defense establishments of ASEAN as a robust US presence is necessary for peace and stability in Southeast Asia and in the broader Indo-Pacific Region," he said during the ASEAN-United States Defence Ministers' Informal Meeting in Lapu-Lapu City, Cebu.

US Department of War Secretary Pete Hegseth attended the meeting, held on the sidelines of the 20th ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting.

"We are delighted to host this important gathering this year as it coincides with the 80th anniversary of the establishment of our diplomatic ties with the United States. In that spirit, we extend our appreciation to the Honorable Secretary Pete Hegseth and members of his team for joining us here in Cebu on this momentous occasion," Teodoro said. 

The defense chief also expressed appreciation for the United States’ steadfast support for ASEAN centrality and its participation in ASEAN-led mechanisms, including the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) and the second ASEAN-United States Maritime Exercise held in Indonesia in December 2025.

He also expressed elation for the US’ support for the Philippines and Japan as co-chairs of the current cycle of the ADMM-Plus Experts Working Group on Maritime Security.

"We particularly appreciate US participation through (their Navy) and their Air Force in the joint cooperative activity that we hosted in Subic last month," he added.

Teodoro said these  initiatives offered meaningful opportunities to strengthen maritime partnerships and people-to-people ties in support of peace and stability in Southeast Asia and a free and open Indo-Pacific.

"For our part, the Philippines hopes to build on these efforts in the years to come because all of us have relied and will continue to rely on freedom of navigation for the security, prosperity, and resilience of our people," he added.

Hegseth, in turn, hailed the DND chief for his "clarity, leadership, and great work as chairman of the ADMM-Plus over the past year."

"You've continued to showcase the kind of leadership we expect and have come to really appreciate from the Philippines, so thank you very much. And to all our other friends and partners here as members of ASEAN and the ADMM-Plus, we look forward to building on the great foundation that has existed for quite some time," he said.

Earlier this year, Hegseth described a vision of  "a more stable, secure, and prosperous Pacific.”

On Wednesday, he said this vision was “based on strength, built not on wishful thinking but on the backs of strong, self-reliant nations. Nations capable of defending their own sovereignty and contributing to the favorable balance of power that benefits us all.” (Priam F. Nepomuceno/PNA)

ASEAN DEFENSE MEETING. Secretary of National Defense Gilberto C. Teodoro Jr. presides over the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers' Meeting (ADMM) in Lapu-Lapu City, Cebu, on Wednesday (Oct. 28, 2026). The Philippines' chairship coincides with the 50th Anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia, as well as the 20th Anniversary of the ADMM. (Dept. of National Defense photo)

Rassie Erasmus has named six uncapped players in a 37-man Springbok squad for the November leg of the Nations Championship, with Cheslin Kolbe, Eben Etzebeth, Andre Esterhuizen and Handre Pollard ruled out through injury, SA Rugby announced Wednesday.

Stormers flyhalf Yaqeen Ahmed and Bulls flyhalf Luan Giliomee were called up as cover with Pollard missing. Sebastian de Klerk, Markus Muller, Riley Norton and Emmanuel Tshituka are the other new faces, and Erasmus noted that Norton, Giliomee and Ahmed were part of Junior Springbok squads that won the Junior World Championship.

"We've had all six players on our radar for a while now, and they've delivered consistently for their respective franchises in the last two seasons, so they thoroughly deserve their call-ups," Erasmus said.

Of the injured players left out of the travelling squad, Erasmus said: "It's always sad to lose players of that calibre, but we are pleased with the cover we have in those positions, and it also offers other players the opportunity to put up their hands."

Siya Kolisi, Malcolm Marx, Pieter-Steph du Toit and Damian de Allende are among the experienced players in the group, which also includes Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu and Manie Libbok at flyhalf.

Why it matters: South Africa top the Nations Championship's Southern Hemisphere standings on points difference, level with New Zealand on 15 points, and the Tests against Italy on Nov. 7, France on Nov. 13 and Ireland on Nov. 21 lead into Finals Weekend in London from Nov. 27-29, according to SA Rugby.

Erasmus is pictured in a file photo during a South Africa training session at Johannesburg Stadium on July 8, 2026.

text:
Your Guide to Animal-Centered Cozy Fiction
 #cozymystery #horses #dogs
A good **guide to animal-centered cozy fiction** starts with one happy truth: the animal should be more than a cute face on the cover. Whether the story features a sharp-eyed cat, a determined terrier, a retired racehorse, or a parrot with an unfortunate talent for repeating secrets, the animal belongs in the heart of the tale. It brings comfort, humor, and often the one clue a human sleuth might overlook.

For readers who love small-town mysteries and four-legged characters, animal-centered cozies offer a particularly satisfying kind of escape. There is usually a close-knit community, an intriguing crime, a clever amateur sleuth, and enough warmth to make you want to settle in with a cup of tea and a dog at your feet. The mystery matters, but so do the relationships - including the one between a person and an animal who knows them better than almost anyone.

## What Makes a Cozy Mystery Animal-Centered?

Animals appear in plenty of mysteries, but animal-centered cozy fiction gives them real purpose. They may notice a strange scent, lead their person toward an overlooked location, react to someone suspicious, or provide a little comic relief when the questioning gets too serious. Even when the animal does not solve the crime, it helps shape how the sleuth sees the world.

In a cozy, that role should feel natural rather than magical. A dog may recognize that a visitor has been near the scene of a crime because of a familiar scent. A cat may slip into a room no human can enter. A veterinarian, groomer, wildlife rehabilitator, or pet sitter may have knowledge that brings animal welfare and human motives together. These details create opportunity for smart clues without asking readers to suspend all common sense.

The best stories also understand that animals are individuals. A nervous rescue dog will not behave like a confident police K-9. A food-motivated beagle may be brave in the presence of a dropped sandwich and less enthusiastic about a dark shed. Those quirks are not decorations. They make the animal memorable and can make a clue feel earned.

## The Warmth Comes With Stakes

Cozy mysteries are known for inviting settings, but cozy does not mean consequence-free. Someone has been harmed, a community is unsettled, and the amateur sleuth has a reason to keep asking questions. Animal-centered stories add an extra layer of feeling because readers naturally worry about the creature caught in the middle.

That does not mean every book needs endangered pets or a threatened farm. In fact, repeated peril can become exhausting. Often, the strongest stakes are personal: a beloved shelter could close, a dog’s owner is wrongly suspected, or a local event that supports animal rescue is being sabotaged. These concerns keep the story tender without losing the mystery’s edge.

A satisfying cozy balances tension with reassurance. The reader can enjoy a suspicious alibi, a missing heirloom, or a muddy paw print while trusting that the book will not become bleak. There may be danger, but there is also a safe place to return to - a kitchen, clinic, bookstore, porch, stable, or small town where people show up for one another.

### The Animal Cannot Be Only a Plot Device

Readers can tell when a fictional animal has been added merely to sell a mystery. If the dog appears in chapter one, disappears for most of the book, and returns only to bark at the killer in the final pages, the relationship may feel thin.

Look for stories where the animal has an ongoing presence. It may interrupt an interview at the worst possible moment, insist on a daily walk that leads to neighborhood gossip, or offer quiet companionship after a difficult discovery. A well-written animal companion affects the rhythm of the sleuth’s day. That is often where the humor and heart live.

For animal lovers, believable care matters, too. Readers do not need a veterinary textbook, but they appreciate authors who respect an animal’s needs, body language, and limits. A little accurate observation goes a long way. It makes the cozy world feel trustworthy.

## How to Choose Animal-Centered Cozy Fiction

Start with the kind of animal relationship that appeals to you. Some readers want a talking or narrating animal with a lively point of view. Others prefer a traditional human narrator whose pet is a loyal sidekick. Neither approach is better; they simply offer different pleasures.

An animal narrator can bring deliciously funny misunderstandings. A dog may know which person smells frightened but have no idea why humans care so much about paperwork. A cat may judge every visitor’s manners with great confidence. This perspective makes familiar mystery scenes fresh because the animal notices sensory details people miss.

A human-led story, on the other hand, often makes room for deeper professional knowledge or community connections. A veterinarian might understand injuries, medications, or behavior that changes the direction of an investigation. A shelter volunteer may know every pet owner in town. A groomer may overhear more than customers realize. These careers can supply useful clues while keeping the sleuth grounded in a caring daily life.

Consider the setting as well. A coastal Florida town, mountain village, historic downtown, horse country, or lakeside community each gives animal fiction its own flavor. The setting should do more than provide a pretty backdrop. It should influence the mystery through local history, seasonal events, wildlife, weather, and the ways neighbors know one another’s business.

## A Reader’s Guide to Animal-Centered Cozy Fiction Clues

The animal-related clue is most satisfying when it is specific, fair, and not too convenient. If a dog finds a crucial object, the reader should understand why the dog was there and why that object matters. If a cat reacts badly to a suspect, there should be more behind it than feline intuition alone.

Good animal clues often involve ordinary details made meaningful: an unusual treat, a changed walking route, a missing medication, burrs caught in fur, a gate left unlatched, or the scent of a place where someone claimed they had never been. These clues work because they arise from routine. The sleuth notices them not by superhuman brilliance, but by paying attention.

Canine forensics can be especially fun when handled with care. Dogs experience the world through scent, sound, movement, and routine. Their observations may point a human investigator in the right direction, but the human still has to connect the evidence. That partnership keeps the mystery clever. The dog contributes a warm snout and remarkable senses; the sleuth contributes questions, judgment, and the courage to follow through.

## Look for Community, Not Just Cuteness

The strongest animal-centered cozies understand that pets and animals create community. Dog walkers meet before breakfast. Clients gather at a veterinary office. Volunteers trade rumors at an adoption event. Children visit a farm. Neighbors step in when an older resident’s pet needs care. These everyday connections offer both plausible suspects and genuine affection.

This is where the cozy mystery earns its emotional payoff. The solution restores more than order. It helps mend trust in a neighborhood, family, or friendship circle. The animal often becomes the gentle thread running through that repair, reminding readers that kindness can be practical as well as sentimental.

Of course, not every book needs a perfect town full of perfect people. A little gossip, rivalry, and old-fashioned stubbornness make the suspects more entertaining. The key is that the story treats its community with affection. Even flawed characters should feel like people who belong to the place.

## Let Your Reading Mood Lead the Way

If you want a lighter read, choose a cozy with a playful pet, a familiar setting, and a mystery centered on local events or personal disputes. If you prefer more puzzle, look for a series with an observant animal companion, recurring suspects, and clues rooted in a believable profession. Readers who enjoy a bit of history may gravitate toward towns with old homes, forgotten landmarks, and secrets that have stayed buried for years.

It also helps to sample a series with the expectation that relationships grow over time. In the first book, you are learning the town, the sleuth, and the animal’s habits. By later installments, a favorite dog’s greeting or a cat’s disapproving stare can feel like visiting an old friend. That familiarity is one of cozy fiction’s special comforts.

Animal-centered cozies invite readers to keep their eyes open for small details, trust the wisdom of a devoted companion, and enjoy the company along the way. Choose a story with a mystery that piques your curiosity, an animal you would gladly spend an afternoon with, and a town you will be sorry to leave when the last clue falls into place.

#threatreport:
The campaign impersonates the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida and sends personalized phishing emails to more than 100,000 companies. Each message uses a fabricated Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) case identifier and links to a tailored page on `https://t.co/O42J9hI5D3`. The site presents a fake case portal and offers a password-protected ZIP archive, with the ADR ID serving as the password. The archive contains an ISO with three disguised delivery files: an MMC file, a batch file, and a shortcut. Each ultimately installs the same LodaRAT variant under a different name: `Taskmgr.exe`, `SystemSettings.exe`, or `msedge.exe`.

The payloads are AutoIt-based LodaRAT builds downloaded from the typosquat domain `https://t.co/0U9eJnp4aV`. They share a cleartext TCP command-and-control channel to `https://t.co/FGESuCxd3K`, the same command set, and similar execution and persistence behavior. The malware copies itself into `%APPDATA%\Windata`, creates persistence through a Startup shortcut, Run key, and scheduled task, and uses a watchdog. It also collects system details and can disable Windows Defender through group policy registry settings.

LodaRAT supports extensive remote access and data theft. It can steal browser credentials and cookies, Firefox profile files, FileZilla server details, Wi-Fi keys, and supplied DPAPI data. Other capabilities include keylogging, screen and webcam capture, microphone recording, shell and file operations, clipboard access, and remote control. It can enable RDP, create an administrator account, establish an ngrok tunnel, provide SOCKS proxying, and spread across network shares or USB drives.

The phishing site is restricted to Microsoft Edge user agents. The report identifies `https://t.co/kLW8V1i37Y` as hosting a bulk-email platform that may have been used to send the messages. The RAT’s C2 resolves to `207.148.77.235`; the phishing and payload infrastructure is hosted separately. The three builds use different campaign tags but share enough code and behavior to indicate a common builder or operator.

Noah Wyle Reveals a Fan Asked Him to Examine Her Fresh Surgical Stitches Because She Thought He Was a Real Doctor

“I was sitting in this restaurant with my wife and another couple, and this older couple came to the table and said, ‘I’m so sorry to bother you, but we just have to tell you we love The Pitt. We haven’t missed an episode yet.’”

“‘I just had surgery, would you mind taking a look?’”

Wyle said the woman then rolled up her pant leg and showed him “the freshest stitches I’ve seen in a long time.”

“She said, ‘What do you think?’ And I said, ‘It looks like it’s healing nicely. Are you putting full weight on it?’ And she said, ‘I am.’”

He then looked up to find his wife staring at him like, “Are you doing this right now?”

When asked if people actually think he’s a real doctor, Wyle admitted:

“Oh, absolutely. And occasionally I do too.”

“I’m always kind of amused by it when people come up and actually think that I can offer real medical advice.”

text:
The city zoned nine-tenths of a Black neighborhood away from housing, then called the place unfit for housing. That was the East Harlem Triangle in 1961, six thousand people on eighty-five acres New York wanted to fill with four million square feet of factory floor instead.

The residents turned down every politician, social worker and clergyman who offered to speak for them, counted their own blocks door to door until they knew the neighborhood better than the Planning Commission did, and went downtown to say so themselves.

The only place the children of the East Harlem Triangle had to play was the strip under the elevated Harlem River Drive and the ground around the Triborough Bridge approaches. When the neighborhood surveyed itself in 1968, it wrote down that traffic coming off those bridges had killed several of its children in the past year, and that parents kept sending their children out there because there was nowhere else to send them.

The people who wrote that down were the Triangle Association. By then they had already spent seven years arguing with the City of New York about whether anybody should be living on those blocks at all.

The Association began in 1961 as the Committee for the Preservation of the East Harlem Triangle and later incorporated as the Community Association of the East Harlem Triangle. Everybody inside it just said the Triangle Association.

The Triangle they were named for was eighty-five and a half acres. It ran from 125th Street up to the Triborough Bridge, with the railroad tracks down Park Avenue on one side and the Harlem River Drive on the other.

Six thousand people lived on it in 1960. Sixty percent were Black, twenty percent Puerto Rican, and twenty percent white.

In the late fifties the city told them the Triangle was going to get new housing. They waited.

Then in May of 1961 the City Planning Commission announced it was studying the Triangle for light manufacturing, and put its finding in writing. The area was one of the most blighted and run-down places in Harlem, the commission wrote, and "wholly unsuitable for housing."

The plan was more than four million square feet of industrial floor space. Housing would be permitted in a thin band around the edges, the way you leave a rind.

Nobody in the Triangle found that out from a newspaper. A church told them.

Chambers Memorial Baptist sat on the boundary and had members living inside the lines. Its pastor since 1958 was Melvin Schoonover, a white minister who did his work from a wheelchair, and his church called a public meeting to tell the neighborhood what the city had written about it.

That meeting is where the Triangle Association came from.

The people in that room made a decision that sounds like nothing and was everything. They decided the only way to survive the City of New York was to know more about the Triangle than the city knew.

So they built a file.

An anonymous private grant paid for a headquarters at 130 East 129th Street, a small staff, and a file of information on households and neighborhood conditions. People who lived on those blocks kept adding to it, year after year, while the buildings around them came down.

Then they carried it downtown.

Politicians offered to speak for them at the hearings. Social workers offered, and so did clergymen.

The Triangle Association turned every one of them down and sent residents to testify in front of the Planning Commission and the Board of Estimate themselves.

They said four things, over and over, for years.

They said the city had undercounted the people it was about to move, and had ignored that most Triangle families were already locked out of public housing, which was the city's own answer for where the displaced would go. They said an honest plan had to start with what those families needed and not with what the land could be worth.

They said the population had barely moved in years, which meant people were staying on purpose.

And they said that whatever the paperwork downtown claimed, there was a real community on those blocks, built out of neighbors who accepted each other and looked out for each other.

It took months of negotiation to move the city an inch, and the inches were real. The industrial designation was amended so that housing could go on the edges of the Triangle.

Code enforcement started years ahead of the usual schedule, a new school was promised inside the Triangle, and the Association won a seat in the study, the planning and the execution of whatever came next.

The people kept leaving while the concessions were being won.

Inside six years the Triangle lost at least a third of its people. Buildings were condemned, families were written up for overcrowding, land was taken for public facilities, and every one of those was a legal reason for somebody to leave and never be let back.

The code enforcement program the Association had fought to win, the one meant to stop landlords letting buildings rot, got used more often to empty the buildings than to fix them.

The delays did the same work. Two years went by while the city negotiated with a sociologist who was supposed to study the neighborhood, and the Triangle kept shrinking the whole time.

Every time the Association got a working relationship with a housing official, the man was promoted or dropped, and they started over with a stranger.

In December of 1965 the Association walked into a room full of city commissioners and asked for something nobody in New York had asked for before. They asked to hold the contract for the study of their own neighborhood.

The commissioners said yes. The Association's own account records its astonishment, and its suspicion that the city agreed mostly because the results might come in handy in other neighborhoods it considered a problem.

Six weeks later the whole administration changed and the men who had signed were gone. Association representatives carried the signed agreement into the new commissioner's office and told him the city was going to honor it.

The city honored it.

Over the summer of 1966, nine people from the Triangle sat down with a planner from the Architects' Renewal Committee in Harlem, and kept sitting down with him, day after day, through the heat. They drew maps of their own blocks and marked what was actually on them, which was not what the zoning maps said.

The Architects' Renewal Committee had been founded in 1964 to give planning help to people who could never afford it. By 1968 it was led by J. Max Bond, who would go on to design the Schomburg Center and the King Center in Atlanta, and its staff was Black.

The survey opened on the second of October, 1967. Surveyors photographed and graded every building in the Triangle, then sent a second team inside a hundred of them to check the first team's work, because the Association knew the city would go looking for a reason to throw the numbers out.

There were 278 buildings. Of the 148 that people actually lived in, 143 were substandard or seriously deficient, and 75 of those had gone up before 1920.

But the file had already turned up the number that broke the city's sentence in half.

Streets and alleys took up more than a third of the Triangle's land, and non-residential uses took another forty percent.

Housing was allowed on eleven percent of the ground.

The city had zoned almost the entire Triangle for manufacturing, left one-ninth of it for human beings, watched what that did to the buildings, and then declared the place unsuitable for housing.

The file kept going, and it got harder to read.

Income in the Triangle came to about $1,250 a year per person. That was more than a quarter below the figure for Mississippi, which was the poorest state in the country.

Among Triangle young people under twenty-one and out of school, thirty-seven percent had no work at all, and among the Black ones it was 58.8 percent, twice the national rate for Black teenagers. The ones who did have jobs averaged $67.80 a week.

Eight hundred and forty children in the Triangle were under five years old, and there was not one day care center. Four hundred and twenty people were over sixty, and there was nowhere for them to sit down together.

Doctors would not make house calls in the Triangle. More than half the heads of household got their only medical care in the emergency room at Harlem Hospital, and about half of them had been hospitalized in the previous year.

On the fifteenth of June, 1968, the Harlem Eye and Ear Hospital inside the Triangle closed. Its own physicians kept the doors open part-time afterward, on their own time, because otherwise there was nothing.

The same survey counted the storefronts. White owners held about 85 percent of the stores in a neighborhood that was 70 percent Black, and hired from outside it.

Among the factories and shops, more than forty percent of employers said they would not train Black or Puerto Rican workers even when the training would have cost them nothing, while naming labor shortage as one of their two biggest problems.

Three out of four former residents the surveyors tracked down said they wanted to come home if they could find a rent they could pay.

So the Association built the plan around that.

New housing would go up on the empty land first, and every family would move once, straight out of an old apartment into a finished new one. Seventeen numbered steps, worked out on paper, so that nobody would be stored anywhere in between.

They had watched relocation used as a way to make neighbors disappear, and they wrote the plan so it could not be done to them again. The plan calls the official promise that displaced people get first pick of the new apartments exactly what it was, which is a cruel joke.

And then they redrew the roads.

The plan closed 125th Street to through traffic, closed three residential blocks to cars, and put a new ramp at the Third Avenue Bridge to send Bronx traffic straight down the Harlem River Drive instead of through 128th Street. It was written by people who had been told downtown that traffic has to keep moving if the city is going to survive.

Their answer to that argument, in print, is that the men who make it do not have to watch their own children cross a street underneath a bridge ramp.

They also said they were done accepting the kind of second-class planning that had already given Harlem its towers and its junior high schools built without windows. They wanted the planning ideas that had built America's suburbs turned on their own blocks instead.

All of it went into one report. It says white people had been asking Black people for a long time what it was they wanted, and that these sixty-nine pages are the answer to that question.

The report is dated August 1968. Alice Kornegay is listed on it as president, and she had come to East Harlem at ten years old from Georgetown, South Carolina, to live with cousins after her parents died.

Its second page is a list of names, and the report says most of the credit for its accuracy belongs to them. Rosa Brown, Helen Griffin, Julia Turner, Beatrice Gaines, Blondell Brito, Keron Moon, Norris Hill, Lenora Thompson, Olga Rivera, Elaine Austin, Sixto Rosario.

Not one of them was a planner. They were people from the neighborhood who had gone door to door.

Late in 1968, with the report in hand, the city approved a goal of 2,400 new apartments for the Triangle, 1,600 of them for low-income families.

The plan the file had built was never put up.

One development came out of it, at Lexington between 128th and 129th. It opened with 189 apartments, sixty percent of them set aside for older people because the Association would not sign off otherwise, and the rent came to thirty-seven dollars a room against the ninety dollars a room people had been paying nearby.

Bond's firm designed it. The tenants named it for Jackie Robinson.

The rest died in Washington. The Association had two eleven-story buildings and a thirteen-story building lined up behind it, 603 apartments between them, and in 1973 the federal government froze the subsidy money.

It froze it after the old buildings had already come down and the families and the businesses had already been moved off the land.

The freeze lifted in 1976. The Association came back with a smaller ask, opened two more buildings on Triangle blocks in 1979, and went on putting up housing, day care, senior apartments and social services on that ground into the next century, long after Kornegay died in 1996.

Nobody ever got the neighborhood the file described. What the Triangle got instead was thirty years of building it back one address at a time, on eighty-five acres the City of New York had declared unfit for anybody to live on.

The report is scanned now and anyone can open it. Go to the second page before you read anything else, because that is where the eleven names are, and in fifty-eight years hardly anybody has gone looking for them.

Then read what the Association wrote about its own neighbors, who had stopped believing that housing would ever get built for them there. It said there was one breath of hope left in the Triangle, and that "breath of hope is themselves."

They were the only ones who had ever slept there.

#Spain faced drought long before most of Europe, and it has turned that experience into a head start. I sat down with @el_pais in Madrid to talk about it.

As I see it, when you are on the frontlines of climate disruption, you adapt faster and you become a standard bearer for others to follow. Spain already recycles 15% of its wastewater; meanwhile, many other European countries, including France, are still below 1%. Spain has become a global laboratory for water innovation, with the solutions developed now exported to 45 countries. 

So, why recycle #water exactly? Around Murcia, by supplying farmers with treated wastewater, we ease tensions between water users. In Catalonia, we go one step further as we turn it into drinking water.

Simply put, the solutions exist, and their payoff is now undeniable. This is why we are accelerating even more in Spain, with €1 billion in investments targeted by 2030.
Energy is an equally essential part of the equation. When a town or factory produces its own power from often overlooked resources such as waste heat or non-recyclable waste, it becomes much better insulated from geopolitical shocks and price spikes.

And there is now a new player entering the resource sovereignty arena: AI and its data centers, key to Europe’s digital future. Data centers do consume huge amounts of energy and water to cool servers; however, with our recently unveiled Data Center Resource 360 offer, we can cut their freshwater use by up to 75%. 

We’re already putting this approach into practice on the ground. In Mississippi, for example, we’re partnering with Amazon Web Services to transform treated municipal wastewater into cooling water for data centers, with operations set to begin in 2027. We also have the ability to recover the heat from these facilities to warm nearby homes through district heating networks. At the end of the day, this is how data centers will earn their place in local communities.

These are all critical resource topics that transcend politics and will be shaping future economic decisions for decades to come. And that is why we are fully confident when we plan for the very long term in places like Spain.

Spain is like few other countries in Veolia’s culture and history. We have been here since 1867, nearly 160 years, and we fully intend to stay for at least another 160!

text:
The World's Three Major Airline Alliances: Star Alliance, SkyTeam, and oneworld

In today's aviation industry, no single airline can realistically serve every major city on Earth. To expand their global reach while reducing costs and improving customer convenience, airlines have formed powerful international partnerships known as airline alliances. Three alliances dominate global aviation: Star Alliance, SkyTeam, and oneworld. Together, they account for well over half of global airline traffic and connect thousands of destinations worldwide.

What Is an Airline Alliance?

An airline alliance is a cooperative arrangement among airlines that allows them to:

Coordinate schedules
Share airport facilities and lounges
Offer reciprocal frequent-flyer benefits

Revenue Expansion

Receive elite-status recognition throughout the alliance

Final Assessment

If judged by sheer size, network reach, passenger traffic, and combined revenue, Star Alliance remains the global leader, serving more countries and carrying more travelers than any competing alliance.

SkyTeam occupies the middle position, benefiting from the powerful Delta-Air France-KLM-Korean Air network and a balanced mix of domestic and international traffic.

oneworld, though the smallest of the three, arguably has the strongest concentration of premium international carriers and is particularly appealing to long-haul business and luxury travelers through airlines such as British Airways, Qatar Airways, Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, and Qantas.

Together, these three alliances form the backbone of modern global aviation, enabling travelers to reach nearly every corner of the world using a single ticket, a single loyalty program, and a seamless travel experience.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
October 28, 2026
Veterans for America First Endorses South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson for Governor

SOUTH CAROLINA — Veterans for America First (VFAF), also known as Veterans for Trump, proudly announces its endorsement of South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson for Governor. The endorsement was announced by VFAF National President Robert Cornicelli, who praised Wilson's military service, leadership, commitment to constitutional principles, and dedication to protecting South Carolina families and veterans.

Wilson, a combat veteran who served in Iraq, has risen to the rank of Colonel in the South Carolina National Guard and is anticipated to receive a promotion to Brigadier General. His military career reflects decades of leadership, discipline, and service to the nation.

As South Carolina's Attorney General, Wilson has built a record of defending constitutional freedoms, supporting law enforcement, protecting families, and advocating for public safety.

"Alan Wilson is more than a public servant. He is a combat veteran, a military leader, and a man who understands the meaning of service, sacrifice, and commitment to our country," stated Cornicelli.

Cornicelli, who works directly with veterans facing homelessness, eviction, unemployment, and other serious challenges, emphasized the importance of electing leaders who recognize the continuing needs of America's military veterans and their families.

"Far too many veterans who proudly served our nation are now struggling to keep a roof over their heads, provide for their families, or find meaningful employment. We need leadership that recognizes these challenges and is willing to bring government, communities, and organizations together to create real solutions," Cornicelli said.

"I believe Alan Wilson understands that our responsibility to those who served does not end when they take off the uniform. It is a lifelong commitment, and one that must be reflected in the priorities of our state government."

Cornicelli concluded, "South Carolina needs a Governor who knows how to lead, understands sacrifice, and puts service above politics. Alan Wilson has spent his life demonstrating those qualities. I am proud to stand with Alan Wilson and offer my full endorsement for Governor of the great state of South Carolina."

About Veterans for America First (VFAF)

Veterans for America First, also known as Veterans for Trump, is a national grassroots organization established in 2015 that brings together military veterans, law enforcement professionals, and patriotic Americans dedicated to supporting constitutional freedoms, veterans' interests, national security, and America First leadership. The organization actively participates in political endorsements, voter engagement, public policy advocacy, and veteran outreach initiatives nationwide.

Wednesday, October 28, 2026 — Week 9

Conference USA Wednesday Night Doubleheader

Tonight's two nationally televised games feature Kennesaw State visiting Middle Tennessee and Jacksonville State traveling to New Mexico State.

The primary handicapping considerations are quarterback execution, offensive-line protection, defensive personnel, rushing efficiency, turnover creation and whether recent final scores accurately reflect the quality of each team's performance.

WEATHER AND GAME CONDITIONS
Weather does not presently appear likely to materially disrupt either contest.
Murfreesboro, Tennessee: Forecasts indicate mild conditions with light winds, approximately 2–5 mph. There is no indication of sustained winds approaching the 15-mph threshold that would make downfield passing and kicking more difficult.

Las Cruces, New Mexico: Temperatures are projected around 70 degrees near kickoff, with light winds around 2 mph. Conditions should be favorable for passing, punting and field-goal attempts.

Neither game currently presents a significant weather-based argument for reduced offensive efficiency. Any late change in wind speed deserves attention, particularly in Las Cruces, where an open stadium can expose the kicking game.

GAME 1: KENNESAW STATE AT MIDDLE TENNESSEE

7:00 PM ET — CBS Sports Network

Records: Kennesaw State 1-6 (0-3 CUSA); Middle Tennessee 4-3 (2-1 CUSA)

QUARTERBACK PERSONNEL: KENNESAW STATE'S MOST IMPORTANT QUESTION

Kennesaw State's quarterback situation is a significant development entering Wednesday.

Rickie Collins has been the primary starter, but coach Jerry Mack turned to Landon Varnes during last Thursday's 34-6 loss to Liberty.

Collins completed 15 of 26 passes for 124 yards with two interceptions. Varnes completed 9 of 15 for 111 yards without an interception.

That is a meaningful difference in efficiency:

Varnes generated more passing yardage per attempt, but the circumstances matter. His production came after the offense had already struggled and the game situation had changed.
The sample is too small to establish that Varnes is the better quarterback. Nevertheless, the difference warrants attention.
Collins had been considerably more productive in the two previous conference games, throwing for 293 yards against Jacksonville State and 260 against Missouri State.
He completed 50 of 68 passes across those two contests, a 73.5% completion rate.
That suggests the Liberty performance may not represent his normal effectiveness against Conference USA defenses.
Personnel impact: A change to Varnes could alter the offensive playbook, particularly quarterback-designed runs, protection calls and downfield passing concepts. A return to Collins would offer greater continuity but also bring renewed scrutiny of his ball security.
The starting decision had not been conclusively established in the available morning reports.

KENNESAW STATE RECEIVING CORPS

Two potential availability concerns involve wide receiver Zion Booker and tight end Gerard Bullock Jr.

Both have appeared on injury listings with undisclosed ailments, although the available reports do not establish that either will miss Wednesday's game.

Booker is an important underneath receiving option. His availability matters because an inexperienced or newly installed quarterback benefits from dependable short-area targets.

Bullock's situation could affect both the passing game and the protection structure. Tight ends can provide additional pass protection, chip edge rushers and serve as quick outlets against pressure.

If either player is unavailable, the effect could be magnified by the uncertainty at quarterback.

A receiver's absence is not simply a subtraction of catches and yards. It can force remaining personnel into unfamiliar alignments, reduce formation flexibility and allow defenses to concentrate coverage elsewhere.

MIDDLE TENNESSEE QUARTERBACK ROMAN GAGLIANO

Middle Tennessee has a more established quarterback situation.

Roman Gagliano enters after consecutive conference victories, producing:

Against Delaware: 22-of-32 passing, 291 yards, three touchdowns and one interception.

Against Florida International: 16-of-27 passing, 200 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions.

Across those two victories, Gagliano completed 38 of 59 passes for 491 yards, four touchdowns and one interception.

His 64.4% completion rate and 8.3 yards per attempt represent a more encouraging offensive profile than the team's season-long statistics suggest.

However, Gagliano also completed only 9 of 26 passes for 81 yards during the 55-0 loss to Kansas.

The contrast is substantial. Against Kansas, Middle Tennessee could not sustain offensive possessions or consistently execute its passing game. Against Delaware, Gagliano produced explosive efficiency.

The personnel and matchup question is whether Kennesaw State can reproduce the coverage pressure that stronger opponents have generated against the Blue Raiders.

MIDDLE TENNESSEE TIGHT END AVAILABILITY
Tight end T. Galloway has been listed as questionable with an undisclosed injury.

His final status remains important for offensive personnel packages, particularly short-yardage and red-zone formations.

If Galloway cannot participate, Middle Tennessee may have to redistribute tight-end snaps or use more receiver-heavy formations.

That could reduce blocking flexibility against a Kennesaw State defense that has been more competitive against the run than Middle Tennessee's own defense.

The most interesting matchup is Kennesaw State's rushing offense against Middle Tennessee's rushing defense.
Middle Tennessee is allowing nearly 195 rushing yards per game, ranking near the bottom of the FBS.
Kennesaw State, however, has not demonstrated consistent rushing production against FBS opposition.
The Owls rushed for 197 yards against Arkansas State but managed only 117 against Jacksonville State, 77 against Missouri State and 62 against Liberty.
Their rushing totals have deteriorated substantially during conference play.
This is an important distinction between a theoretical matchup advantage and one a team has demonstrated the personnel to exploit.
If Kennesaw State can establish Latrelle Murrell and its other backs early, it can reduce the burden on whichever quarterback starts.
If Middle Tennessee forces repeated second-and-long and third-and-long situations, the quarterback uncertainty becomes more damaging.
DECEPTIVE FINAL SCORES: KENNESAW STATE
Kennesaw State's 1-6 record deserves additional examination.

Three of its recent defeats came by a combined seven points:

The Jacksonville State and Missouri State losses are especially interesting because Collins threw for a combined 553 yards.
Kennesaw State also generated 410 total yards against Jacksonville State and 337 against Missouri State.
Those results suggest an offense capable of moving the ball without consistently translating that production into victories.
However, the Liberty defeat was different. The Owls produced 297 total yards, including only 62 rushing yards, and failed to score a touchdown.
The distinction matters. The close losses provide evidence that Kennesaw State has been competitive, but the Liberty result raises legitimate questions about whether its offensive performance is deteriorating.
A misleading record is not automatically an indication of an improving team. In this case, both explanations must be considered.
THIRD DOWNS, RED ZONE AND TURNOVERS
Middle Tennessee's third-down conversion rate is only 25.6%, among the lowest nationally.
That creates a potentially important opportunity for Kennesaw State to force punts, shorten drives and keep the game competitive.
Kennesaw State has also been undisciplined, averaging 71.6 penalty yards per game, compared with 52.4 for Middle Tennessee.
Middle Tennessee owns a plus-five turnover differential, compared with an even differential for Kennesaw State.
Another concern for the Owls is red-zone defense. Opponents have scored on approximately 96% of their red-zone opportunities.
Middle Tennessee's own red-zone offense has not been particularly efficient, scoring on 81.3% of its trips.

The matchup therefore involves two weaknesses rather than a clear strength against a weakness.

MOTIVATION AND SITUATIONAL FACTORS

Kennesaw State won the Conference USA championship last season but enters this game with six consecutive losses.

At 1-6, the Owls must win their remaining five regular-season games to reach six victories.

Middle Tennessee has won two consecutive conference games and remains involved in the league race.

The motivational profiles differ. Kennesaw State is attempting to salvage a disappointing season, while Middle Tennessee has a realistic opportunity to build on its recent conference momentum.

Both teams are playing on shortened preparation schedules, although Middle Tennessee has an additional two days of rest after playing Florida International on October 20, compared with Kennesaw State's October 22 game against Liberty.

That difference could be important if either coaching staff makes meaningful personnel or schematic adjustments.

BETTING PERFORMANCE

Middle Tennessee is 5-2 ATS, while Kennesaw State is 4-3 ATS.

Those records reinforce the distinction between outright performance and performance relative to expectations.

Kennesaw State has lost six games but has covered four of seven contests. Middle Tennessee has covered five of seven despite a negative season-long scoring differential.

The ATS records alone do not establish the quality of either team. The more useful question is whether the current market sufficiently accounts for Kennesaw State's close defeats and Middle Tennessee's defensive limitations.

Game-defining personnel questions: Kennesaw State's starting quarterback, the availability of Booker and Bullock, Galloway's status for Middle Tennessee, and whether the Owls can protect their quarterback well enough to exploit the Blue Raiders' vulnerable run defense.

GAME 2: JACKSONVILLE STATE AT NEW MEXICO STATE

8:00 PM ET — ESPN2

Records: Jacksonville State 5-2 (3-0 CUSA); New Mexico State 3-4 (2-1 CUSA)

NEW MEXICO STATE RUNNING BACK JAMES JONES: THE CENTRAL PERSONNEL MATCHUP

New Mexico State running back James Jones is arguably the most consequential offensive player in Wednesday's doubleheader.

Jones enters with 777 rushing yards, averaging 111.0 yards per game. He has exceeded 100 rushing yards four times and leads Conference USA in rushing production.

His recent performance has been particularly impressive.

Against Sam Houston last Wednesday, Jones rushed for a career-high 178 yards and a touchdown on 27 carries.

That is 6.6 yards per attempt despite a substantial workload.

Jones has averaged 140.7 rushing yards across New Mexico State's three conference games.

This is not merely a case of one running back producing big numbers behind an explosive offense. New Mexico State's offensive identity has changed dramatically.

The Aggies finished last nationally in rushing offense in 2025, averaging just 2.60 yards per carry.

This season, that figure has improved to 4.58 yards per carry, with the offense averaging 151.4 rushing yards per game.

Personnel impact: Jones' vision and patience are particularly valuable against Jacksonville State's aggressive defensive structure.

New Mexico State frequently employs inside-zone and Duo rushing concepts, which depend on offensive-line movement, patient running and exploiting developing gaps.

Jones is effective at waiting for blocks to develop rather than immediately attacking the first visible opening.

That skill becomes especially important against a defense that frequently sends additional rushers.

JACKSONVILLE STATE LINEBACKERS: A POTENTIAL DEFENSIVE VULNERABILITY

Jacksonville State's run defense has allowed approximately 4.7 yards per designed rushing attempt, with opponents producing a 44.1% rushing success rate.

Two individual linebackers deserve scrutiny.

Jameson McCollough has played 213 defensive snaps, but his reported PFF run-defense grade is only 40.8.

Marvin Stringfellow has played 197 snaps and has been credited with 13 missed tackles.

Those numbers are significant because New Mexico State's running game emphasizes patience, blocking angles and second-level opportunities.

If Jones consistently reaches the linebackers without being contacted near the line of scrimmage, missed tackles could produce substantial gains.

Jacksonville State coach Charles Kelly has acknowledged the difficulty of defending the Aggies' rushing attack.

The defensive adjustment may involve more aggressive run fits, additional defenders near the line of scrimmage and greater emphasis on gap discipline.

However, committing additional personnel against the run can create opportunities for play-action passes and one-on-one receiving matchups.

NEW MEXICO STATE QUARTERBACK ADAM DAMANTE

New Mexico State made a significant quarterback change earlier this season, replacing Trey Hedden with Adam Damante.

Damante has started the last four games.

The offense has become more comfortable with him operating the system, although New Mexico State remains more dependent on rushing production than passing efficiency.

Damante threw two touchdown passes to AJ Williams III in last week's 30-24 victory over Sam Houston.

Williams finished with three receptions for 52 yards and two touchdowns.

The development is encouraging because it demonstrates the offense can convert passing opportunities into touchdowns without requiring a large number of attempts.

Nevertheless, the Aggies' overall passing statistics remain modest.

New Mexico State has completed approximately 56% of its passes and continues to struggle with turnovers.

The team has committed 18 offensive turnovers through seven games.

Damante also threw an interception against Sam Houston that coach Tony Sanchez characterized as a correctable decision-making error.

Personnel impact: Damante must recognize Jacksonville State's pressure packages and avoid holding the football when protection breaks down.

Jacksonville State blitzes on approximately 48.5% of defensive snaps, an unusually aggressive rate.

That pressure can create opportunities for negative plays, hurried throws and interceptions.

But it also creates openings for quick passes, screens and explosive plays if Damante identifies the pressure correctly.

The Aggies' offensive success may depend less on Damante producing exceptional passing yardage and more on avoiding costly mistakes.

JACKSONVILLE STATE QUARTERBACK CADEN CREEL

Jacksonville State quarterback Caden Creel provides a different offensive challenge.

The Gamecocks have produced a passing success rate of approximately 55%, completing nearly 68% of their passes while averaging 8.6 yards per attempt.

Those are strong efficiency indicators.

Creel is also involved in the rushing attack, adding another dimension to Jacksonville State's offensive structure.

New Mexico State must account for the quarterback on designed runs and broken plays.

That responsibility can prevent linebackers from aggressively pursuing running backs and can create favorable angles for Jacksonville State's blocking schemes.

However, the matchup is complicated by New Mexico State's outstanding recent run defense.

The Aggies have allowed just 51.3 rushing yards per game against Conference USA opponents.

That is an exceptionally strong figure, although it must be evaluated in the context of the offenses they have faced.

If New Mexico State can control Jacksonville State's conventional rushing attack without committing additional defenders, Creel may be forced to carry more of the offense through the air.

JACKSONVILLE STATE RECEIVER DEONDRE JOHNSON

Deondre Johnson is an important vertical threat.

Johnson enters with 431 receiving yards and three touchdowns, averaging approximately 19.6 yards per reception.

That explosive-play capability makes him especially dangerous when opponents concentrate on stopping Creel's rushing ability.

A single successful deep pass can offset several unsuccessful possessions.

However, New Mexico State's pass defense has been effective this season.

The Aggies have allowed only five passing touchdowns and primarily employ zone coverage.

Jacksonville State's passing game frequently attacks underneath, including a substantial number of screens and throws behind the line of scrimmage.

This creates an intriguing contrast.

New Mexico State must defend quick passes without allowing Johnson to exploit coverage mistakes downfield.

JACKSONVILLE STATE RECEIVER AND RUNNING BACK INJURIES

Jacksonville State enters with several reported personnel concerns.

Wide receiver AJ Watkins is listed out. Franklin Baret Jr. has appeared on reports with conflicting out/questionable designations.

Other receivers appearing on questionable lists include Rollie Pinto, Landon Watkins, Nabi Hoyt and Gabe Glover.

Running backs Andrew Paul and Justus Savage have also appeared on injury reports. Paul has been identified as out for the season in another report.

These are not all confirmed game-day absences, and the final availability report remains important.

The potential impact is significant.

Jacksonville State uses screens and quick passes extensively. That requires receivers who can execute perimeter blocks, create yards after the catch and recognize defensive leverage.

If multiple receivers are unavailable, Creel may have fewer dependable options for those concepts.

Depth issues could also increase the workload of healthy players, especially in formations using three or four wide receivers.

The bye week has provided additional recovery time, but coach Charles Kelly has acknowledged that the team has lost some players for the season.

NEW MEXICO STATE DEFENSIVE PERSONNEL: SAFETY AND NICKEL DEPTH

New Mexico State's secondary has a noteworthy personnel issue.

Coach Tony Sanchez reported injuries in the safety group, particularly at nickel.

The situation prompted the coaching staff to move true freshman Xavier Rucker from running back to nickel/safety.

Rucker played 30 defensive snaps in the previous game.

That is an important development against Jacksonville State.

The nickel defender is frequently responsible for slot coverage, run support and recognizing screens.

Jacksonville State's offense relies heavily on short passing concepts, meaning its personnel can repeatedly challenge the nickel defender's recognition and tackling.

Rucker's athleticism may help him handle the position, but his relative inexperience could be tested by formations, motion and route combinations.

This is one of the most important individual personnel matchups in the game.

If Jacksonville State can isolate an inexperienced nickel defender, it could generate efficient completions without relying on difficult downfield throws.

Conversely, if New Mexico State's secondary maintains its communication and tackling discipline, the Aggies could limit Jacksonville State's passing efficiency.

NEW MEXICO STATE PASS RUSH: GABE PETERSON

Defensive end Gabe Peterson leads Conference USA with 5.5 sacks.

He has recorded four sacks against conference opponents.

New Mexico State has registered multiple sacks in four consecutive games.

However, Jacksonville State has allowed only approximately one sack per game, among the lowest figures nationally.

This creates a matchup between an effective individual pass rusher and an offense that has generally protected its quarterback.

Two Jacksonville State offensive linemen have relatively weak individual pass-blocking grades.

Tackle Cedric Kouemi has a reported pass-blocking grade of 48.6, while center Lucas Mrachkovskiy has a 56.0 grade.

Peterson's alignment and New Mexico State's pressure design will be important.

If Peterson consistently wins his individual matchup, Jacksonville State may have to use additional blockers or shorten Creel's passing concepts.

That could reduce the number of receivers available downfield.

DECEPTIVE BOX SCORE: NEW MEXICO STATE 30, SAM HOUSTON 24

New Mexico State's six-point victory over Sam Houston was considerably more dominant defensively than the final score suggests.

The Aggies held Sam Houston to just 11 rushing yards and nine first downs.

Those are exceptional defensive figures.

New Mexico State also generated takeaways that produced short scoring opportunities.

Safety Josiah Charles intercepted a pass and returned it to the Sam Houston 1-yard line, setting up a Jones touchdown.

Kaian Roberts-Day recovered a fumble that led to another touchdown.

Three of New Mexico State's five scoring drives lasted no more than two plays and 45 seconds.

However, Sam Houston also returned a blocked punt for a touchdown.

That special-teams score helped keep the final margin relatively close.

The result therefore contains two important handicapping lessons.

First, New Mexico State's defensive performance was stronger than a simple six-point victory might indicate.

Second, the Aggies benefited from unusually favorable field position created by turnovers.

Those short scoring drives do not necessarily establish that New Mexico State can consistently sustain long possessions against stronger opposition.

STRENGTH OF RECENT OPPOSITION

New Mexico State's defensive improvement has been substantial, but its last three opponents have been among Conference USA's least productive scoring offenses.

That makes Jacksonville State an important test.

The Gamecocks bring a more efficient passing game and a quarterback capable of contributing on the ground.

New Mexico State's impressive recent rushing-defense statistics may partially reflect weaker competition.

At the same time, Jacksonville State has not faced a rushing attack quite like the one built around James Jones.

Both teams are therefore confronting personnel and schematic challenges that differ from their recent schedules.

MOTIVATION, REST AND TRAVEL

Jacksonville State enters 3-0 in Conference USA play and is tied with Liberty among the conference leaders.

A victory would preserve its undefeated conference record and secure a sixth win, the standard benchmark for bowl eligibility.

New Mexico State is 2-1 in conference play.

An Aggies victory would bring the teams level at 3-1 and provide New Mexico State with an important head-to-head advantage.

Jacksonville State has not played since October 13, giving the Gamecocks a 15-day break.

That extended rest provides an opportunity for injured players to recover and for the coaching staff to correct execution problems.

However, Jacksonville State must also make a lengthy trip of approximately 1,216 miles to Las Cruces.

The Gamecocks are 1-2 on the road this season.

New Mexico State is 2-1 at home and has emphasized establishing a stronger home-field advantage.

There is also a potential scheduling distraction for the Aggies.

They host Liberty on November 7, creating consecutive home games against two of Conference USA's leading teams.

The opportunity to influence the conference race is substantial, but New Mexico State cannot afford to look beyond Jacksonville State.

RED-ZONE EXECUTION AND TURNOVERS

Jacksonville State has moved the football effectively but has experienced problems finishing drives.

Its reported red-zone touchdown conversion rate is approximately 36.4%.

That is a significant concern because successful drives ending in field goals rather than touchdowns can allow an opponent to remain competitive.

New Mexico State's defense has been effective at limiting explosive passing production, making red-zone execution particularly important.

Turnovers are another concern.

New Mexico State has committed 18 offensive turnovers, while Jacksonville State has committed 13.

Those numbers create meaningful uncertainty in a matchup where both defenses are capable of forcing mistakes.
